_rule: An algorithm appears here only if its source was checked. `source_type` records what kind of source that is: paper (peer-reviewed), article (written up but not published academically), reference-implementation (the code is the specification), or folklore (real, widely used, no canonical origin). The rule was originally paper-only; it was widened because that excluded genuinely important techniques — domain warping, pity timers, falling-sand — and so misrepresented practice as more academic than it is. Filter on source_type to get the strict set back.

algorithms.name: Apollonian gasket
algorithms.authors: Apollonius of Perga; curvature relation by René Descartes
algorithms.summary: Recursively pack circles into the gaps between three mutually tangent circles. Curvatures are integers.
algorithms.eli5: Three coins touching one another leave a curvy triangle of gap between them. Drop in the biggest coin that fits, and you have made three new smaller gaps. Keep going forever. The strange part: if the first three coins have tidy whole-number sizes, so does every coin that ever fits.
algorithms.description: Start with three mutually tangent circles. Descartes' circle theorem gives the curvature of a circle tangent to all three as a simple quadratic in the other three curvatures, with two solutions — the small circle nestled in the gap and the large one enclosing them. Take the small one, and you now have three new gaps; recurse. The construction fills the space with circles whose sizes fall off in a strict pattern, and if the starting curvatures are integers then every curvature in the whole infinite packing is an integer, which is why the object is as much a number-theory result as a geometric one. Visually it is the archetype of non-uniform packing, and the recursion is the reason it appears in procedural art, decorative tiling and any layout that wants organic size variation rather than a grid.
algorithms.citation: Apollonius of Perga, tangency problems; Descartes' circle theorem, 1643

algorithms.name: Catenary
algorithms.authors: Huygens, Leibniz and Johann Bernoulli, independently
algorithms.summary: The curve a uniform chain takes under its own weight. cosh, not a parabola — and the difference is visible.
algorithms.eli5: Hold a chain by both ends and it sags into one very particular curve. Galileo thought it was the same shape as a thrown ball; it is not, and the difference shows up near the ends, which is exactly where the eye goes. Get it wrong and your power lines look mysteriously too shallow.
algorithms.description: A flexible cable of uniform density hanging between two points settles into y = a·cosh(x/a), where a is the ratio of horizontal tension to weight per unit length. Galileo thought it was a parabola; it is not, and although the two are close near the vertex they diverge visibly toward the supports, which is exactly where a viewer's eye goes. That is why hanging cables modelled as parabolas or as plain Bézier curves read as subtly wrong — too shallow at the ends. Inverted, the same curve is the funicular shape of a masonry arch under its own weight, which is why it turns up in thrust-network analysis for compression-only vaults. For generation it is the correct default for any slack cable, power line, rope bridge or drooping wire, and it costs one hyperbolic cosine.
algorithms.citation: Solved independently by Huygens, Leibniz and Johann Bernoulli in 1691, in response to a challenge from Jakob Bernoulli

algorithms.name: Clothoid / Euler spiral
algorithms.authors: Leonhard Euler; rediscovered for rail by Arthur Talbot
algorithms.summary: A curve whose curvature increases linearly with arc length. The correct transition between straight and curve.
algorithms.eli5: You cannot join a straight road straight onto a bend — a driver would have to yank the wheel round instantly. So put a curve in between whose tightness increases steadily as you travel along it, letting the wheel turn at a constant rate. Every real road and railway has one at both ends of every bend.
algorithms.description: Joining a straight line directly to a circular arc creates a discontinuity in curvature — zero on one side, constant on the other. A vehicle following it would need to snap the steering wheel instantly, which is why real roads and railways never do this. The clothoid has curvature proportional to distance travelled, so it interpolates smoothly from zero to the arc's curvature and the driver turns the wheel at a constant rate. Its coordinates are Fresnel integrals with no elementary closed form, so it is evaluated by series or lookup. It is also the correct shape for rollercoaster transitions, for the same comfort reason. Getting this right is most of what makes generated road networks read as engineered rather than drawn — the catalogue's own note that 'the right curve type is most of the realism' is pointing at exactly this.
algorithms.citation: Euler, 1744; applied to railway transition curves by Talbot, 1890

algorithms.name: Lotka–Volterra
algorithms.summary: Two coupled equations for predator and prey. Produces perpetual out-of-phase population cycles.
algorithms.eli5: Two numbers: rabbits and foxes. Rabbits multiply on their own and get eaten in proportion to how often a rabbit meets a fox. Foxes starve on their own and breed in proportion to what they eat. Those two sentences make both populations rise and fall forever, with the fox peak always trailing the rabbit peak.
algorithms.description: Prey grow exponentially in the absence of predators and are eaten at a rate proportional to the product of the two populations; predators starve exponentially without prey and grow in proportion to what they eat. Four parameters, two equations. The result is a closed orbit in phase space — populations cycle forever, with the predator peak lagging the prey peak by a quarter period, which matches observed lynx and hare records well enough to have made the model famous. For world simulation it is the minimal model that produces an ecosystem that feels alive without scripting, and its known unrealism is instructive: the cycles are neutrally stable, so any perturbation permanently changes the orbit and there is no carrying capacity, which is why practical implementations add logistic growth and saturation terms.
algorithms.citation: Lotka, Elements of Physical Biology, 1925; Volterra, Variazioni e fluttuazioni del numero d'individui in specie animali conviventi, 1926

algorithms.name: Aeolian sand transport
algorithms.summary: Wind moves sand by saltation — grains hop and knock others loose. Dunes emerge, with a slip face at the angle of repose.
algorithms.eli5: Sand does not float on the wind, it hops. A grain gets lifted, flies a short arc, and knocks more grains loose where it lands — so below a certain wind speed nothing moves at all, and above it everything does. Bumps shelter the air behind them, sand settles in the shelter, and when the pile gets too steep it avalanches into a dune's sharp face.
algorithms.description: Bagnold established that wind rarely carries sand in suspension; it moves it by saltation, where grains are lifted, travel a short ballistic hop, and on landing eject further grains. The consequence is a threshold: below a critical wind speed nothing moves, above it transport is self-sustaining. Dunes form because a bump shelters its lee side, so sand deposits there, and the deposit grows until its downwind face exceeds the angle of repose and avalanches — producing the sharp slip face that distinguishes a dune from a heap. Procedural implementations are usually a cellular model on a heightfield: probabilistically move sand downwind, then run a repose-angle relaxation pass. It is the same two-stage shape as thermal erosion, and the reason wind direction alone determines whether you get barchans, transverse ridges or star dunes.
algorithms.citation: Bagnold, The Physics of Blown Sand and Desert Dunes, Methuen, 1941

algorithms.name: Simplex method / linear programming
algorithms.summary: Optimise a linear objective under linear constraints by walking the vertices of the feasible polytope.
algorithms.eli5: Your rules carve out a shape with flat sides, like a cut gemstone, and the best possible answer always sits on one of its corners. So stand on a corner, look along each edge leading away from it, and walk to whichever corner is better. Stop when no edge leads anywhere better.
algorithms.description: The feasible region of a set of linear inequalities is a convex polytope, and because the objective is linear its optimum must lie at a vertex. Simplex exploits that: start at a vertex and repeatedly move along an edge to an adjacent vertex that improves the objective, stopping when none does. It has exponential worst case and is fast in practice, which is one of the more famous gaps between theory and behaviour in computing. Adding the requirement that some variables be integers gives mixed-integer programming — enormously harder, but the formulation that actually covers scheduling, routing, packing and allocation. This is the machinery behind most of the `bizops` domain of the catalogue, and the reason those entries produce a provably optimal artefact rather than a plausible one.
algorithms.citation: Dantzig, developed 1947; published in Activity Analysis of Production and Allocation, 1951

algorithms.name: n-gram models
algorithms.summary: Predict the next symbol from the previous n−1. The oldest generative text model, and still the cheapest.
algorithms.eli5: Read a long list of names and tally, for every pair of letters, which letter came next. To invent a name, roll dice weighted by those tallies, again and again. With one letter of context you get gibberish; with two or three you get something that sounds like it belongs on the list.
algorithms.description: Count how often each sequence of n symbols occurs in a corpus, and use those counts as the conditional probability of the final symbol given the n−1 before it. Sampling from that distribution repeatedly generates new text. Shannon introduced it in the paper that founded information theory, and demonstrated it by sampling letter-level and word-level approximations to English of increasing order — the classic illustration that order 0 gives noise, order 2 gives pronounceable nonsense, and order 3 gives something eerily close to language. For generation the practical sweet spot is character-level order 2 or 3 over a name corpus: low enough to invent, high enough to sound like the source. Higher orders simply plagiarise, because with enough context each n-gram has only one observed successor.
algorithms.citation: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication, Bell System Technical Journal 27, 1948

algorithms.name: Strahler stream ordering
algorithms.authors: Arthur Strahler, building on Robert Horton
algorithms.summary: Number every stream by how deep its branching is. Two equal tributaries make the next order up; unequal ones do not.
algorithms.eli5: Every stream with no streams flowing into it is a 1. When two 1s join, the result is a 2. When two 2s join you get a 3 — but when a 2 meets a 1, it is still just a 2. So the number tells you how many times the river has properly doubled, which turns out to be a very good guide to how wide it should be drawn.
algorithms.description: Assign order 1 to every headwater link. At a confluence, if the two highest incoming orders are equal, the outgoing order is one greater; otherwise it is the maximum of the incoming orders. Computed by one upward pass over the flow tree that D8 or D-infinity produced. The scheme is what makes the empirical regularities of river networks measurable — the number of streams, their mean length, and their drainage areas each fall off in an approximately geometric series with order, which is Horton's laws — and that is precisely what a generator needs to look plausible. Practically it is the width and naming dial: order maps to channel width, to whether a crossing needs a ford or a bridge, to how far sound and mist carry, and to which watercourses deserve a name on the map. Its known quirk is the unequal-tributary rule, which means a long trunk can absorb many small tributaries without ever gaining order — a real property of the measure, and the reason the alternative Shreve ordering, which simply adds magnitudes, exists.
algorithms.citation: Strahler, Hypsometric (area-altitude) analysis of erosional topography, Bulletin of the Geological Society of America 63(11), 1117–1142 (1952); ordering scheme refining Horton, Erosional development of streams and their drainage basins, GSA Bulletin 56(3), 1945

algorithms.name: Reaction–diffusion
algorithms.summary: Two substances diffusing at different rates while reacting spontaneously break symmetry into spots and stripes. The mechanism behind animal coat markings.
algorithms.eli5: Two chemicals on a wet sheet. The first makes more of itself wherever it already is — but it also makes the second, which spreads out faster and destroys the first. So every blob of the first chemical digs a moat around itself that stops any other blob forming too close. That fixed spacing is what makes spots spots.
algorithms.description: Two chemicals share a field: an activator that autocatalyses itself locally, and an inhibitor that suppresses the activator but diffuses faster. Short-range activation combined with long-range inhibition means a uniform starting state is unstable — any tiny fluctuation grows into a peak, which then suppresses its own neighbourhood, forcing the next peak to appear a characteristic distance away. That characteristic distance is the pattern's wavelength. Gray–Scott is the usual discretised form: two coupled partial differential equations iterated on a grid, with feed and kill rates as the two parameters. Those two numbers select the entire pattern class — spots, stripes, mazes, or dissolution — and the boundaries between classes are sharp, which is why the parameter space feels like a cliff edge.
algorithms.citation: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 237(641), 37–72. doi:10.1098/rstb.1952.0012

algorithms.name: Kruskal's algorithm
algorithms.summary: Sort every edge by weight and add it unless it would close a cycle. Minimum spanning tree by greed.
algorithms.eli5: Sort every possible connection from cheapest to dearest. Walk down the list building each one — unless the two things it would join are already connected by some other route, in which case skip it. When the list runs out, everything is joined as cheaply as possible and there are no loops.
algorithms.description: Sort all edges by weight, then walk the list adding each edge unless its endpoints are already connected — a union-find structure answers that in near-constant time. The result is a minimum spanning tree, and the greedy choice is provably safe because the lightest edge crossing any cut must belong to some MST. In level generation it is the standard way to connect a set of rooms: build a Delaunay triangulation of room centres, take the MST for guaranteed connectivity with no loops, then add back a small random fraction of the discarded edges to reintroduce loops deliberately. That two-step is what gives dungeons which are connected but not tree-shaped, which is the difference between a layout that reads as designed and one that reads as a maze.
algorithms.citation: On the shortest spanning subtree of a graph and the traveling salesman problem, Proc. American Mathematical Society 7, 48–50

algorithms.name: Prim's algorithm
algorithms.summary: Grow one tree outward, always taking the cheapest edge leaving it. Same result as Kruskal, different shape when randomised.
algorithms.eli5: Start in one room and keep a list of every door leading out of the part you have built. Repeatedly open the cheapest such door and swallow the room behind it. It costs the same in total as the sorting method, but it grows as one spreading blob, which is why it makes bushier mazes.
algorithms.description: Start from a single vertex and repeatedly add the cheapest edge connecting the tree to a vertex outside it, using a priority queue over the frontier. It produces the same minimum spanning tree as Kruskal on distinct weights, but the difference matters when you randomise the weights to generate mazes: Prim's grows outward from a seed, so it produces bushy layouts with many short branches and frequent junctions, whereas the recursive backtracker produces long winding corridors with few. Neither samples the space of mazes uniformly — that needs Wilson's algorithm — but the bias is a design choice rather than a defect, because 'bushy' and 'winding' are legitimately different level feels.
algorithms.citation: Shortest connection networks and some generalizations, Bell System Technical Journal 36, 1389–1401

algorithms.name: De Casteljau's algorithm
algorithms.summary: Evaluate a Bézier curve by repeated linear interpolation between control points. Numerically stable, and splits the curve for free.
algorithms.eli5: To find a point on a curve steered by a few handles: mark the same fraction of the way along each line between consecutive handles, join those marks up into a new set of lines, and do it again. Keep going until one point remains — that point is on the curve. It also hands you both halves of the curve for free.
algorithms.description: Take the control polygon and linearly interpolate along every edge at parameter t, producing a new polygon with one fewer point. Repeat until a single point remains — that point is on the curve. The recursion is the definition of the curve rather than a way of computing a formula, which is why it is numerically stable where direct evaluation of the Bernstein polynomial is not. A side effect is more useful than the evaluation itself: the intermediate points from the two outer chains are exactly the control points of the two sub-curves either side of t, so the same recursion subdivides a Bézier into two Béziers at no extra cost. That is what makes adaptive flattening, curve trimming and intersection testing tractable. De Casteljau developed it at Citroën in 1959; Bézier published later at Renault and got the name.
algorithms.citation: De Casteljau, Citroën technical reports, 1959; see also Bézier's later publication of the same curve family

algorithms.name: Halton sequence
algorithms.summary: Deterministic low-discrepancy sequence giving even coverage of a space, one dimension per prime base.
algorithms.eli5: You want points spread evenly, but you also want to keep adding more without starting over. The trick: write 1, 2, 3… in binary and read each one's digits backwards after the point. Out comes 1/2, then 1/4, then 3/4, then 1/8 — every new point automatically landing in the biggest gap left.
algorithms.description: Each dimension uses a different prime base. The i-th value in a dimension is the radical inverse of i in that base: write i in base p, then reflect its digits about the decimal point. In base 2 the sequence runs 1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/8, 5/8 — each new point landing in the largest remaining gap. Because it is deterministic and incremental you can keep adding samples without recomputing, and coverage stays even at every prefix length, unlike uniform random which clumps. The weakness is that high prime bases correlate visibly with each other, so beyond roughly six dimensions the points fall into stripes and need scrambling.
algorithms.citation: On the efficiency of certain quasi-random sequences of points in evaluating multi-dimensional integrals, Numerische Mathematik 2, 84–90

algorithms.name: Column generation
algorithms.summary: Solve a problem with astronomically many variables by generating only the ones that could improve the solution.
algorithms.eli5: A crew roster has more possible shift patterns than you could ever list. So solve a tiny version using a handful of patterns, read off from that solution which qualities it is starved of, and go hunting for one new pattern that has them. If no such pattern exists, the tiny answer was the real answer all along.
algorithms.description: Some problems have a natural formulation with an impossible number of variables — in cutting stock, one variable per possible way of slicing a roll; in crew scheduling, one per legal roster pattern. Column generation never enumerates them. Solve a restricted problem containing a handful of columns, read the dual prices off that solution, and use them to define a *pricing subproblem* that asks: does any column not yet included have negative reduced cost? If one exists, add it and re-solve; if none does, the restricted solution is optimal for the full problem. The subproblem is usually a knapsack or shortest-path instance, and solving it is how you search a combinatorial space without touching most of it. This is the machinery behind airline crew pairing and industrial nesting.
algorithms.citation: Gilmore & Gomory, A linear programming approach to the cutting-stock problem, Operations Research 9(6), 849–859

algorithms.name: Discrete-event simulation
algorithms.authors: Emerged with GPSS (Geoffrey Gordon, IBM) and SIMULA
algorithms.summary: Advance time by jumping to the next scheduled event, not by fixed steps. The basis of queue and process modelling.
algorithms.eli5: Do not tick the clock through a night when nothing happens. Keep a diary of things that are going to happen, always jump the clock straight to the next entry, do that thing, and let it write new entries further down. Simulating a week of a hospital costs only as much as the events in it.
algorithms.description: Maintain a priority queue of future events ordered by timestamp. Repeatedly pop the earliest, advance the clock straight to it, execute its handler — which typically schedules further events — and continue. Time never ticks through intervals where nothing happens, so simulating a week of a factory or a hospital costs only as much as the events in it. This is the standard machinery for queueing, logistics, manufacturing throughput and service capacity, and it is what sits behind the catalogue's entries on venue ingress, clinic scheduling and warehouse operation. Its assumption is also its limit: the state may only change at events, so anything genuinely continuous has to be either discretised into events or handled by a hybrid solver.
algorithms.citation: No single origin paper. Emerged through GPSS (Gordon, IBM, 1961) and SIMULA (Dahl & Nygaard, 1962).

algorithms.name: Wang tiles
algorithms.authors: Hao Wang; first aperiodic set by Robert Berger, 1966
algorithms.summary: Square tiles with coloured edges that may only abut when colours match. Some sets tile the plane only aperiodically.
algorithms.eli5: Square tiles with a colour painted on each edge. Two tiles may sit side by side only if the touching edges are the same colour. You never have to look at the whole picture to place a tile, only at its neighbours — and a handful of tiles can cover an unlimited area with no obvious repeat.
algorithms.description: Each tile is a unit square with a colour on each of its four edges, and two tiles may sit side by side only if the touching edges match. Wang conjectured in 1961 that any set able to tile the plane could also tile it periodically; his student Robert Berger disproved this in 1966 by constructing an aperiodic set of 20,426 tiles, later reduced by others to a handful. The practical value in graphics is that a small set of edge-matched tiles produces unbounded non-repeating coverage from a tiny asset budget, and the matching rule is purely local — you can decide any tile from its neighbours without global search, which is why Wang tiling underlies stochastic texturing and terrain tiling.
algorithms.citation: Wang, Proving theorems by pattern recognition II, Bell System Technical Journal 40, 1961; Berger, The undecidability of the domino problem, 1966

algorithms.name: DPLL
algorithms.authors: Martin Davis, George Logemann, Donald Loveland
algorithms.summary: Backtracking search over boolean assignments with unit propagation. The core of every SAT solver since.
algorithms.eli5: Guess that some true-or-false variable is true. Follow the consequences: any rule left with only one unsettled option forces that option, which forces others. If you hit a contradiction, back up and guess false instead. Nearly every modern solver is still this, plus careful bookkeeping about *why* each failure happened.
algorithms.description: Pick an unassigned variable, guess a value, and propagate the consequences: any clause reduced to a single unassigned literal forces that literal, which may force others, cascading. If propagation produces a contradiction, backtrack and try the other value. That loop — decide, propagate, backtrack — is still the skeleton of modern solvers, which add conflict-driven clause learning (on failure, derive a new clause explaining why, so the same dead end is never re-entered), non-chronological backjumping, and activity-based variable ordering. Those additions are what took SAT from a theoretical curiosity to something that routinely handles millions of variables. For generation it matters because 'make me content satisfying these hard constraints' reduces to SAT surprisingly often — solvable puzzles, valid layouts, legal tile adjacency.
algorithms.citation: Davis, Logemann & Loveland, A machine program for theorem-proving, CACM 5(7), 394–397

algorithms.name: Sobol sequence
algorithms.summary: Base-2 low-discrepancy sequence built from direction numbers, faster and better-behaved in high dimensions than Halton.
algorithms.eli5: The same idea, with a cleverer recipe that keeps working when you need many directions at once. Where the simple version starts falling into stripes past a handful of dimensions, this one keeps its even spread, which is why it is what rendering and finance actually use.
algorithms.description: Works entirely in base 2. Each dimension carries a set of 'direction numbers' derived from a primitive polynomial over GF(2), and successive points are produced by XORing the current point with the direction number corresponding to the lowest unset bit of the index. Because the whole generator is bit operations it is extremely fast, and the construction guarantees that every aligned dyadic box contains its fair share of points. It holds up far better than Halton in high dimensions, which is why it is the default for quasi-Monte Carlo integration and for sampling in renderers.
algorithms.citation: On the distribution of points in a cube and the approximate evaluation of integrals, USSR Comput. Math. and Math. Physics 7(4)

algorithms.name: A*
algorithms.authors: Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson, Bertram Raphael
algorithms.summary: Best-first graph search guided by a heuristic estimate of remaining cost. Optimal if the heuristic never overestimates.
algorithms.eli5: When hunting for a route, always explore the option with the best "distance walked so far, plus a guess at the distance still to go". As long as the guess never overestimates, the moment you reach the goal you are guaranteed to have the shortest path — having looked at far fewer places than a blind search would.
algorithms.description: Expand nodes in order of f = g + h, where g is the cost already paid to reach a node and h is an estimate of what remains. The estimate is what separates it from Dijkstra: with h = 0 it degenerates to Dijkstra and explores in all directions, while a good h pulls the search straight toward the goal. Optimality requires the heuristic to be admissible — never overestimating the true remaining cost — and consistency additionally guarantees no node is expanded twice. Straight-line distance is the standard admissible heuristic on a map. It matters to generation in two directions: as the thing that consumes generated space, since a navmesh or dungeon graph exists to be searched, and as a validator, since asking whether a path exists at all is how you verify a generated level is completable before shipping the seed.
algorithms.citation: Hart, Nilsson & Raphael, A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths, IEEE Trans. Systems Science and Cybernetics 4(2), 100–107

algorithms.name: fBm / octave summation
algorithms.authors: Benoît Mandelbrot, John Van Ness (as fractional Brownian motion)
algorithms.summary: Sum octaves of a noise function at halving amplitude and doubling frequency. The default "natural" look.
algorithms.eli5: One layer of noise gives soft lumps. Add a second at half the size and half the strength, then a third, then a fourth. The first layer decides the mountains and the last decides the gravel, which is how a couple of lines of arithmetic end up looking like a landscape.
algorithms.description: Evaluate a noise function several times, each at double the previous frequency and a fraction of the previous amplitude, and add the results. That fraction — persistence — controls how much fine detail survives relative to coarse structure, and it is the discrete analogue of the Hurst exponent in Mandelbrot and Van Ness's fractional Brownian motion, which is where the statistical justification comes from: real terrain, coastlines and cloud edges measure as approximately self-affine, so a signal built to have the same spectral slope reads as natural. Two derived operators sit on the same loop: taking the absolute value and inverting gives ridged multifractal, producing sharp crests instead of rounded hills, and squaring gives billow. It is worth being clear that fBm imitates the statistics of erosion and tectonics without containing either.
algorithms.citation: Mandelbrot & Van Ness, Fractional Brownian Motions, Fractional Noises and Applications, SIAM Review 10(4), 422–437

algorithms.name: L-systems
algorithms.summary: Parallel string rewriting, originally describing algal cell division. Interpreted as turtle graphics it produces plants, vessels and space-filling curves.
algorithms.eli5: Start with the letter A and a rule: "A becomes AB". A few rounds later you have a long word. Hand the word to a turtle holding a pen — A means go forward, B means turn, a bracket means remember this spot and come back to it later — and the growing word draws a plant.
algorithms.description: An alphabet of symbols, a starting string called the axiom, and a set of production rules. Each generation, every symbol in the string is rewritten simultaneously — the parallelism is the point, and it is what distinguishes an L-system from a Chomsky grammar, because it models cells dividing at the same time rather than a sequential derivation. After n generations the string is read as turtle commands: F draws forward, + and − turn, and square brackets push and pop the turtle's state to make branches. Stochastic variants attach probabilities to competing rules for the same symbol; parametric variants let symbols carry numbers, so a rule can branch on length or age.
algorithms.citation: Mathematical models for cellular interaction in development, I and II. J. Theoretical Biology 18, 280–299 and 300–315

algorithms.name: Sobel gradient operator
algorithms.summary: Estimate the slope of a field with two 3×3 kernels, one per axis. How a normal map gets made from a heightfield.
algorithms.eli5: To find which way a bumpy surface is tilted at some point, compare the heights to its left and right, and above and below — but give the samples directly beside it more weight than the diagonal ones. Two little three-by-three stencils, one for each direction, and together they give you the direction of steepest uphill.
algorithms.description: Two 3×3 kernels, each the outer product of a [1 2 1] smoothing along one axis with a [−1 0 1] difference along the other, giving the horizontal and vertical partial derivatives in one pass each. The smoothing is what distinguishes it from a plain central difference: it suppresses the single-pixel noise that a raw difference amplifies, at the cost of slightly blurring the edge location. The two outputs form the gradient vector, whose magnitude is edge strength and whose direction is the surface tilt. In procedural texturing this is the standard heightfield-to-normal-map conversion, and the same operator supplies the slope input that drives biome selection, talus and snow placement, wear masks in crevices, and any rule of the form "only where the surface is steep". Sobel and Feldman presented it in a 1968 talk at the Stanford AI Lab; the first printed description is in Duda and Hart's 1973 textbook, which is why it has no conventional paper citation.
algorithms.citation: Sobel & Feldman, A 3×3 isotropic gradient operator for image processing, talk at the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Project, 1968 — never formally published. First in print in Duda & Hart, Pattern Classification and Scene Analysis, Wiley, 1973, 271–272.

algorithms.name: Conway's Game of Life
algorithms.authors: John Conway; popularised by Martin Gardner
algorithms.summary: Four rules on a grid of live and dead cells, producing gliders, oscillators and universal computation.
algorithms.eli5: Each square is alive or dead. Count its eight neighbours: two or three living neighbours and it stays as it is, exactly three and a dead square comes to life, anything else and it dies. Those two sentences are enough to build a working computer inside the grid.
algorithms.description: Every cell on an infinite grid is alive or dead, and updates simultaneously based only on its eight neighbours: a live cell with two or three live neighbours survives, a dead cell with exactly three becomes alive, everything else dies. That is the entire specification. From it come stable blocks, oscillators, gliders that travel, glider guns that emit them indefinitely, and eventually constructions proving the system is Turing complete. Its importance for generation is the demonstration itself — that a rule you can write on a napkin, iterated, produces structure nobody designed and nobody can shortcut predicting. Every cave generator and falling-sand engine is working the same principle at a lower ambition.
algorithms.citation: Gardner, Mathematical Games: The fantastic combinations of John Conway's new solitaire game 'Life', Scientific American 223, 120–123

algorithms.name: Quadtree and octree
algorithms.authors: Alexander Klinger (region quadtree); name from G. M. Hunter; octree from Donald Meagher
algorithms.summary: Recursively split space into four (or eight) equal children, subdividing only where there is detail.
algorithms.eli5: Cut a square into four. If a quarter is boring — entirely empty or entirely full — stop there. If it is interesting, cut it into four again. You end up spending detail only where there is detail to spend it on, which is how one structure can hold a whole country and a single street.
algorithms.description: Divide a square into four equal quadrants; subdivide any quadrant that still contains more than you want, and stop where it does not. The octree is the same in three dimensions with eight children. Because the split is always at the midpoint, a node's bounds are implied by its path from the root — no coordinates need storing, and a position maps to a leaf by reading bits of its coordinates. That gives cheap neighbour queries, level-of-detail for free (a node is a valid coarse approximation of its subtree), and adaptive resolution that costs memory only where detail exists. In generation it underlies sparse voxel worlds, terrain LOD, collision broad-phase and image quantisation. Its weakness is that axis-aligned midpoint splits ignore the data's actual shape, so badly aligned content produces deep, unbalanced trees. The attribution is worth getting right because two different structures share the name. Finkel and Bentley's 1974 quadtree splits at data points, for retrieval on composite keys; the structure described here — split always at the midpoint, subdivide where there is detail — is the region quadtree, which is Klinger 1971, given this name by Hunter in 1978, and extended to three dimensions as octree encoding by Meagher in 1980. Graphics and generation use the region variety almost exclusively.
algorithms.citation: Klinger, Patterns and search statistics, 1971 (region quadtree); Hunter, Efficient computation and data structures for graphics, PhD thesis, Princeton, 1978 (the term "quadtree" in this sense); Meagher, Octree encoding, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute technical report IPL-TR-80-111, 1980. Finkel & Bentley, Quad trees: a data structure for retrieval on composite keys, Acta Informatica 4, 1–9 (1974) is the *point* quadtree, a different structure.

algorithms.name: Shape grammars
algorithms.summary: Rule-driven rewriting of geometric configurations. Introduced to specify paintings and sculpture; later the basis of procedural architecture.
algorithms.eli5: Rules that rewrite shapes instead of words: "wherever you see this square, replace it with these two rectangles". Keep applying whichever rules match, and a plain starting shape turns into a facade, a floor plan or a piece of ornament.
algorithms.description: Rules take the form 'wherever this labelled shape appears, replace it with that shape'. Unlike string grammars the matching is geometric, so a rule fires on any occurrence under translation, rotation, reflection or scale. The architectural descendant is the split grammar: a rule subdivides a labelled volume along an axis into labelled parts, so a building mass splits into floors, a floor splits into facade tiles, a tile splits into window, sill and wall. Because each rule only sees its own scope, the whole building is described by a page of rules rather than a model.
algorithms.citation: Shape grammars and the generative specification of painting and sculpture, Proc. IFIP Congress '71

algorithms.name: De Boor's algorithm
algorithms.authors: Carl de Boor (with M. G. Cox)
algorithms.summary: The B-spline generalisation of de Casteljau. Evaluates a spline of any degree from its knot vector, with local control.
algorithms.eli5: The same repeated-blending trick, but for a curve made of many joined segments where each handle only influences the stretch of curve near it. That locality is the entire point: moving one handle changes a small part of a long curve instead of reshaping the whole thing.
algorithms.description: B-splines are defined by the Cox–de Boor recursion: a basis function of degree k is a weighted blend of two of degree k−1, bottoming out in indicator functions on knot intervals. De Boor's algorithm evaluates the curve directly from that recursion, interpolating between control points with weights derived from the knot vector rather than from t alone. The practical consequence is local support — each control point influences only a span of the curve set by the degree, so moving one vertex does not disturb the whole shape, which is exactly what Bézier curves fail to give you as degree rises. Non-uniform knot spacing lets you place sharper and flatter regions deliberately, and repeating a knot reduces continuity there, which is how you put a deliberate corner in an otherwise smooth curve. NURBS adds per-point weights on top, making conic sections exactly representable.
algorithms.citation: de Boor, On calculating with B-splines, J. Approximation Theory 6, 50–62 (1972)

algorithms.name: Winged-edge and half-edge structures
algorithms.summary: Store each edge with pointers to its neighbours so that "what is next to this?" is answered in constant time.
algorithms.eli5: A list of triangles tells you the shape but not the neighbourhood — to find what is next to a triangle you would have to search the whole list. So store, with every edge, which edges continue around each side of it. Now walking around a corner, or all the way round a face, is just following arrows.
algorithms.description: A bare list of vertices and faces cannot answer adjacency questions without a search. The winged-edge record stores, for each edge, its two endpoints, its two adjacent faces, and the four edges that continue clockwise and anticlockwise around each of those faces — the "wings". From that you can walk the ring of edges around a vertex or around a face in time proportional to the answer rather than to the mesh. The half-edge structure that later replaced it in practice splits each edge into two opposing directed halves, which removes the case analysis the wings require at the cost of doubling the records. Almost every mesh operation in generation needs this and quietly assumes it: edge collapse for decimation, edge split for subdivision, region growing for UV charts, and any traversal that has to stay on a surface. It is also where non-manifold geometry stops being an abstract worry — these structures cannot represent three faces meeting at one edge at all.
algorithms.citation: Baumgart, Winged edge polyhedron representation, Stanford AI Laboratory memo AIM-179 / CS-TR-72-320, 1972

algorithms.name: FM synthesis
algorithms.summary: Modulate one oscillator's frequency with another at audio rate. A few parameters produce very complex evolving spectra.
algorithms.eli5: Take a tone. Now wobble its pitch, thousands of times a second, using a second tone. Once the wobble is fast enough your ear stops hearing wobble and starts hearing an entirely new instrument — bell, brass, electric piano — out of two plain tones and a couple of numbers.
algorithms.description: Take a carrier oscillator and vary its frequency with a second oscillator running at audio rate rather than as a slow vibrato. The result is a set of sidebands at the carrier frequency plus and minus integer multiples of the modulator frequency, with amplitudes given by Bessel functions of the modulation index. Raising the index pushes energy outward into higher sidebands, so a single time-varying parameter sweeps the whole timbre from pure to bright to clangorous. The ratio between carrier and modulator frequency decides whether the sidebands land on harmonics — integer ratios sound like instruments, irrational ratios sound like bells and metal. Chowning's discovery became the Yamaha DX7 and, with it, most of the 1980s.
algorithms.citation: The synthesis of complex audio spectra by means of frequency modulation, J. Audio Engineering Society 21(7), 526–534

algorithms.name: Graph grammars
algorithms.authors: Hartmut Ehrig, Michael Pfender, Hans Jürgen Schneider
algorithms.summary: Rewriting rules over graphs rather than strings. Used to generate mission structure before geometry.
algorithms.eli5: The same rewriting idea, except what gets rewritten is a set of dots joined by lines. A rule says "wherever you find this little arrangement, swap it for that one". Good for building the *plot* of a level — which key opens which door — before anything has a shape at all.
algorithms.description: A rule specifies a subgraph pattern and a replacement; applying it finds a match and substitutes, with a defined discipline for reattaching the dangling edges — the double-pushout construction being the standard formalisation. Unlike string grammars the structure being rewritten has no linear order, which is exactly what you want when the thing you are generating is a network of relationships rather than a sequence. In level design this is the basis of mission-then-space generation: write rules over an abstract graph of goals, locks, keys and rewards, expand until the mission is the desired size and complexity, then embed that graph into geometry as a second step. Separating the two is what lets you guarantee solvability — the mission graph is verifiable before any room exists.
algorithms.citation: Ehrig, Pfender & Schneider, Graph-grammars: an algebraic approach, 14th Annual Symposium on Switching and Automata Theory, 1973

algorithms.name: Catmull–Rom splines
algorithms.summary: A cubic spline that passes through its control points, with tangents derived from the neighbours.
algorithms.eli5: You have a list of points the curve must actually pass through, rather than handles tugging at it from a distance. This picks the direction to leave each point by looking at the point before and the point after. Simple, goes exactly where you told it, and a little prone to overshooting on sharp turns.
algorithms.description: B-splines approximate their control points; Catmull–Rom interpolates them, which is what you want when the points are positions something must actually visit — a camera path, a road centreline, a keyframed value. Each segment is a cubic Hermite curve whose tangent at a point is taken from the vector between its two neighbours, so the whole curve is determined by the points alone with no tangent authoring. The uniform parameterisation has a well-known failure: unevenly spaced points produce overshoot and cusps, where the curve loops outside its own control polygon. The centripetal variant, parameterising by the square root of chord length, provably eliminates both, and is the version worth implementing.
algorithms.citation: Catmull & Rom, A class of local interpolating splines, in Computer Aided Geometric Design, Academic Press, 317–326

algorithms.name: Penrose tiling
algorithms.summary: Two tiles with matching rules that cover the plane only aperiodically, with five-fold symmetry.
algorithms.eli5: Two diamond shapes with markings on them, and one rule: the markings must line up. You can cover an infinite floor with them, but you can never find a patch that repeats like wallpaper. Every finite piece of the pattern turns up again and again elsewhere, and yet the whole never quite repeats.
algorithms.description: Penrose reduced Berger's thousands of aperiodic tiles to two — in the common form, a fat and a thin rhombus, with matching rules enforced by notches or arc markings that forbid the periodic arrangements the shapes alone would allow. The resulting tilings never repeat under translation yet are far from random: every finite patch recurs infinitely often, and the ratio of fat to thin tiles converges to the golden ratio. They also exhibit five-fold rotational symmetry, which is impossible in a periodic tiling, and their discovery in physical quasicrystals a decade later won a Nobel Prize. For generation the appeal is coverage without visible repeat, at the cost of not being able to compute a tile from a coordinate in constant time.
algorithms.citation: Penrose, The role of aesthetics in pure and applied mathematical research, Bull. Inst. Math. Appl. 10, 1974

algorithms.name: Genetic algorithm
algorithms.summary: Encode candidates as chromosomes, select by fitness, recombine and mutate. The founding search-based method.
algorithms.eli5: Write down a hundred random attempts as strings of numbers. Score them, bin the worst, and make the next hundred by splicing two survivors together and flipping the odd digit. Repeat. Nobody ever has to know how to build a good one — only how to recognise one.
algorithms.description: Represent each candidate solution as a string — the chromosome — and maintain a population of them. Each generation, select parents with probability weighted by fitness, produce children by crossover (splicing two parents' chromosomes) and mutation (perturbing symbols), and replace the population. Crossover is the part that distinguishes it from hill-climbing: it assumes good solutions are built from recombinable partial solutions, so mixing two decent parents can produce something better than either. For content generation the appeal is that you only need to *score* quality, not construct it — which is exactly the situation for balance, difficulty and aesthetics, where you can recognise a good result but cannot write down how to build one. The standard failure is convergence: the population collapses onto one local optimum and variety dies, which is what quality-diversity methods were invented to fix.
algorithms.citation: Holland, Adaptation in Natural and Artificial Systems, University of Michigan Press, 1975

algorithms.name: k-d tree
algorithms.summary: Binary space partition that splits on one axis at a time, cycling through dimensions. The workhorse for nearest-neighbour queries.
algorithms.eli5: Split a cloud of points with one straight cut, alternating horizontal and vertical, always cutting so that half the points fall on each side. Repeat inside each half. Finding the point nearest to somewhere now means walking down a few levels instead of measuring against everything.
algorithms.description: At each level, split the point set with a hyperplane perpendicular to one axis, cycling or choosing the axis of greatest spread, usually at the median so the tree stays balanced. Nearest-neighbour search descends to the leaf containing the query, then backtracks, pruning any subtree whose bounding slab is further away than the best candidate found so far — which is what turns a linear scan into a logarithmic one in practice. Unlike a quadtree the split position adapts to the data rather than sitting at the midpoint, so clustered points do not produce degenerate depth. It degrades in high dimensions, where nearly every subtree has to be visited, which is the usual reason people fall back to approximate methods.
algorithms.citation: Bentley, Multidimensional binary search trees used for associative searching, CACM 18(9), 509–517

algorithms.name: Floyd–Steinberg dithering
algorithms.summary: Error diffusion: quantise a pixel, then push the resulting error onto neighbours not yet processed.
algorithms.eli5: You only have black and white ink but you need to print grey. For each dot, use whichever ink is closer — then remember exactly how much you cheated, and push that debt onto the neighbouring dots you have not printed yet. They pay it off, so the average comes out right.
algorithms.description: Scan the image in raster order. Quantise each pixel to the nearest available level, then take the error — the difference between what you wanted and what you got — and distribute it to the not-yet-visited neighbours in fixed proportions: 7/16 to the right, 3/16 down-left, 5/16 down, 1/16 down-right. Because the error is carried forward rather than discarded, local average brightness is preserved exactly, and the eye integrates the scattered dots back into the original tone. Floyd and Steinberg found those four weights by trial and error, choosing them so that a region of half density resolves into a clean checkerboard. The characteristic artefact is a faint diagonal worm pattern in smooth gradients, which is why blue-noise and ordered alternatives exist.
algorithms.citation: An adaptive algorithm for spatial grey scale, Proc. Society for Information Display 17, 75–77

algorithms.name: AC-3 arc consistency
algorithms.summary: Prune values that cannot participate in any solution, propagating until nothing changes. The engine underneath WFC.
algorithms.eli5: Prune before you search. If some value for A has no partner left in B that satisfies the rule between them, that value of A is dead — delete it. Deleting it may kill options for A's other neighbours, so put those back on the queue and keep going until nothing more can be deleted.
algorithms.description: Maintain a worklist of constraint arcs. For each arc, remove from one variable's domain any value with no supporting value in the other's domain — a value that cannot possibly work. If a domain shrinks, re-queue every arc pointing into that variable, because its neighbours' support may have vanished too. Repeat until the queue empties. The result is not a solution but a much smaller search space, and if any domain empties there is provably no solution. It is worth recognising that this *is* Wave Function Collapse: the superposition of tiles in a cell is a domain, collapsing is assigning, and the propagation step is arc consistency. WFC's contradictions are exactly the empty-domain case, which is why it needs backtracking or restart — a property inherited from the constraint literature rather than discovered.
algorithms.citation: Mackworth, Consistency in networks of relations, Artificial Intelligence 8(1), 99–118

algorithms.name: Smoothed particle hydrodynamics
algorithms.authors: Robert Gingold, Joseph Monaghan (independently Leon Lucy)
algorithms.summary: Represent fluid as particles carrying mass, and interpolate every field with a smoothing kernel over neighbours.
algorithms.eli5: There is no water — only a few thousand blobs, each asking its neighbours how crowded things are. Too crowded and it pushes away, and all that pushing is what makes the crowd behave like a fluid. Nothing needs a grid, so the water is free to slosh anywhere it likes.
algorithms.description: There is no grid. Fluid is a cloud of particles, and any quantity at a point — density, pressure, velocity — is estimated by summing contributions from nearby particles weighted by a smoothing kernel that falls to zero at a fixed radius. Density comes from how crowded the neighbourhood is, pressure from density via an equation of state, and force from the pressure gradient, which is itself the analytic gradient of the kernel. Because it is purely Lagrangian, mass is conserved exactly and free surfaces need no tracking, which is why it dominates splashes and pouring. Its weaknesses are also structural: incompressibility is only approximate unless you add a pressure solve, and surface particles have incomplete neighbourhoods, so surface tension and thin sheets are persistently awkward. Invented for astrophysics, borrowed by graphics twenty-five years later.
algorithms.citation: Gingold & Monaghan, Smoothed particle hydrodynamics: theory and application to non-spherical stars, MNRAS 181, 375–389

algorithms.name: BSP trees
algorithms.authors: Henry Fuchs, Zvi Kedem, Bruce Naylor
algorithms.summary: Recursively split space by arbitrary planes, usually taken from the geometry itself. Gives an exact, viewpoint-independent depth ordering.
algorithms.eli5: Take any wall and split the entire world into what is in front of it and what is behind. Do it again inside each half using another wall. Because "in front" and "behind" can never mix, you can walk the tree from any viewpoint and get everything in exact back-to-front order without sorting anything.
algorithms.description: Pick a plane — traditionally the plane of one of the polygons in the scene — and split everything into what lies in front and what lies behind, recursing on each side and splitting any polygon that straddles it. The result is a tree that can be traversed from any viewpoint to yield the polygons in exact back-to-front order, computed once and reused for every frame, which is why it powered early 3D engines before depth buffers were cheap. Unlike quadtrees and k-d trees the splitting planes are arbitrary rather than axis-aligned, so the partition follows the geometry exactly. That exactness is what makes it a solid-modelling structure as well as a rendering one. The cost is fragmentation: a badly chosen plane order can split the scene into far more fragments than it started with.
algorithms.citation: Fuchs, Kedem & Naylor, On visible surface generation by a priori tree structures, SIGGRAPH '80, 124–133

algorithms.name: Gaussian blur (separable convolution)
algorithms.authors: No origin publication; the Gaussian is from Gauss, its use as an image filter is standard practice
algorithms.summary: Blur by weighting neighbours with a bell curve. Separable, so the cost is 2n rather than n² per pixel.
algorithms.eli5: To soften a picture, replace each dot with a weighted average of the dots around it, weighting nearby ones more using a bell-shaped curve. The trick that makes it cheap: blurring left-to-right and then top-to-bottom gives exactly the same answer as blurring in both directions at once, and costs a fraction as much.
algorithms.description: Convolution with a Gaussian kernel is the canonical low-pass filter, and it has two properties that make it the workhorse of every texture pipeline. First it is separable: a 2D Gaussian is the product of two 1D Gaussians, so an n×n kernel becomes two n-tap passes, turning O(n²) per pixel into O(n). Second it is the only rotationally symmetric separable kernel, and it introduces no ringing, because its Fourier transform is another Gaussian with no side lobes — which is why a box blur produces visible artefacts where a Gaussian does not. Successive Gaussians compose into a wider Gaussian by adding variances, so a pyramid of blurs is cheap. In generation it is everywhere and usually unremarked: softening a mask, computing ambient occlusion from a blurred height difference, building the low-frequency half of a detail split, extracting the difference-of-Gaussians band that wavelet noise is built on, and antialiasing any thresholded field.
algorithms.citation: No origin paper. Standard treatment in Gonzalez & Woods, Digital Image Processing; the recursive constant-time formulation is Deriche, Recursively implementating the Gaussian and its derivatives, INRIA RR-1893, 1993.

algorithms.name: Mandelbrot set
algorithms.authors: Benoît Mandelbrot; named by Adrien Douady and John Hubbard
algorithms.summary: Iterate z → z² + c and record which c stay bounded. Infinite structure from five characters of arithmetic.
algorithms.eli5: Pick a number. Square it and add your starting number. Square that and add it again, over and over. Some starting numbers stay small forever and some run off to infinity. Colour in the ones that stay, and the border between staying and running turns out to be infinitely crinkly at every magnification.
algorithms.description: For each point c in the complex plane, iterate z → z² + c starting from zero and ask whether the sequence stays bounded. The set of c for which it does is the Mandelbrot set. Points that escape are coloured by how many iterations they took, which is what produces the familiar bands; smooth colouring uses the fractional escape time to remove the banding, and distance estimation gives clean edges at deep zoom. Its significance for this catalogue is as the extreme case of the compression argument — the generating rule is one line, the structure is genuinely infinite and non-repeating, and no amount of storage could hold what the rule produces. It is also the standard demonstration of the fractal limitation: infinite detail, but self-similar detail, so zooming reveals more of the same rather than anything new.
algorithms.citation: Mandelbrot, Fractal aspects of the iteration of z → λz(1−z), Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 357, 1980

algorithms.name: Recursive backtracker
algorithms.authors: No single origin; depth-first search applied to maze carving
algorithms.summary: Depth-first walk carving passages, backtracking at dead ends. Long winding corridors, few junctions.
algorithms.eli5: Wander at random, digging as you go, never stepping into a cell you have already dug. When you get stuck, retrace your steps until you find a cell with an undug neighbour and set off again. This is the long, winding, few-junctions maze everybody pictures when they hear the word.
algorithms.description: Start at a cell, mark it visited, and repeatedly move to a random unvisited neighbour, carving a passage as you go. When no unvisited neighbour exists, backtrack along the path until one does, and continue. It is depth-first search with the traversal tree taken as the maze, and it is the most commonly implemented maze algorithm because it is six lines and needs no extra structures. Its bias is strong and worth knowing: because it always pushes as deep as possible before backtracking, it produces long, snaking corridors with a low junction count and a high average path length — a very different feel from Prim's bushiness. Neither samples mazes uniformly; only Wilson's algorithm does. There is no origin paper; it is DFS, rediscovered by everyone who has ever written a maze generator.
algorithms.citation: No canonical publication — depth-first search applied to grid carving. Documented in Buck, Mazes for Programmers.

algorithms.name: Bowyer–Watson
algorithms.summary: Incremental Delaunay triangulation. Insert a point, delete every triangle whose circumcircle contains it, retriangulate the hole.
algorithms.eli5: You want to join scattered dots into triangles with no thin splinters. Add the dots one at a time. Each new dot lands inside a few existing triangles — delete exactly those whose circle contains it, which punches a hole, then fan fresh triangles from the dot out to the hole's rim.
algorithms.description: Start with a super-triangle enclosing all points. Insert points one at a time. For each new point, find every existing triangle whose circumcircle contains it — these are exactly the triangles that the new point invalidates. Delete them, which always leaves a single star-shaped cavity, then join the new point to every edge on the cavity boundary. The Delaunay property is restored by construction. Published independently by both authors in the same 1981 issue of The Computer Journal. It generalises to any dimension, and its weakness is numerical: the in-circle test is a determinant that needs exact predicates to avoid producing inconsistent topology on near-degenerate input.
algorithms.citation: Bowyer, Computing Dirichlet tessellations; Watson, Computing the n-dimensional Delaunay tessellation. The Computer Journal 24(2), 1981

algorithms.name: Diffusion-limited aggregation
algorithms.summary: Release random walkers that stick on contact with a growing cluster. Produces dendrites, frost, lightning and coral.
algorithms.eli5: Stick one dot in the middle. Release another far away and let it stagger about at random until it touches the clump, then freeze it there. Repeat. Because the outermost tips catch wanderers first, the clump grows feathery arms and never fills in — which is what lightning, frost and copper deposits look like.
algorithms.description: Seed a single stuck particle. Release a new particle from far away and let it random-walk until it touches the cluster, at which point it sticks permanently; repeat. The resulting aggregate is fractal, with dimension around 1.71 in two dimensions, and it is branched rather than blobby for a reason worth understanding: a walker arriving from outside is overwhelmingly likely to hit a protruding tip before it can diffuse into a fjord between branches, so tips grow faster and shield the interior. That screening effect is the whole mechanism, and it is why the same model describes electrodeposition, mineral veins, frost, lightning channels and coral. Practical implementations cheat the random walk — release walkers from a circle just outside the current radius and take large steps in empty space — because a true walk from infinity almost never arrives.
algorithms.citation: Witten & Sander, Diffusion-Limited Aggregation, a Kinetic Critical Phenomenon, Physical Review Letters 47(19), 1400–1403

algorithms.name: Eller's algorithm
algorithms.summary: Generates a perfect maze one row at a time in constant memory. Infinite mazes with no backtracking.
algorithms.eli5: Build a maze one row at a time and never look back. In the current row, randomly join some side-by-side cells into groups, then make sure every group punches at least one hole down into the next row. You hold only one row in memory at a time, so the maze can be infinitely long.
algorithms.description: Process the maze row by row, holding only the current row. Each cell belongs to a set representing which cells are already connected. Within a row, randomly join horizontally adjacent cells whose sets differ, merging the sets. Then, for each set present in the row, carve at least one vertical passage down to the next row — at least one is what guarantees connectivity, and randomly carving more is what creates variety. Cells in the next row that received no vertical connection start fresh sets. On the final row, join every remaining distinct set horizontally to close the maze. The result is a perfect maze, generated in memory proportional to one row rather than the whole grid, which means the maze can be infinite in one direction — the only classic algorithm with that property. No paper; it circulated through hobbyist programming channels.
algorithms.citation: Marlin Eller, 1982; no original publication — described through hobbyist programming channels and documented in Buck, Mazes for Programmers, Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2015.

algorithms.name: Lloyd relaxation
algorithms.summary: Repeatedly move each site to the centroid of its Voronoi cell. Converges toward evenly sized, rounded cells.
algorithms.eli5: Scattered dots give lumpy, uneven patches. So: for every dot, find the middle of its own patch and move the dot there. Redraw the patches. Do it again. Each round the patches get rounder and more equal, like soap bubbles settling against each other.
algorithms.description: Compute the Voronoi diagram of the current point set, move every point to the centroid of its own cell, then recompute and repeat. It converges toward a centroidal Voronoi tessellation, where each site sits exactly at its cell's centre of mass. Practically, it turns a clumpy random scatter into something that still reads as organic but has no slivers or giant cells — which is the difference between cobblestones that look laid and cobblestones that look spilled. Two or three iterations is usually enough; run it to convergence and the result drifts toward a hexagonal grid and stops looking natural. The same procedure is k-means clustering, arrived at from quantisation rather than geometry; Lloyd derived it at Bell Labs in 1957 but it went unpublished until 1982.
algorithms.citation: Least squares quantization in PCM, IEEE Trans. Information Theory 28(2), 129–137

algorithms.name: Morphological operators
algorithms.summary: Grow, shrink, open and close a region by sliding a shape over it. Set theory rather than arithmetic.
algorithms.eli5: Take a small shape — say a little disc — and slide it over your picture. Everywhere it fits entirely inside the white region, keep the white: that shrinks the region and deletes anything thinner than the disc. Do the opposite and the region grows, filling small holes. Shrink then grow, and specks disappear while everything bigger survives unchanged.
algorithms.description: Two primitives over a structuring element. Erosion keeps a pixel only where the element fits entirely within the region; dilation marks every pixel the element touches. Composing them gives opening — erode then dilate — which deletes anything smaller than the element while leaving larger regions at their original size, and closing, the reverse, which fills small gaps. Because the operations are defined by set containment rather than by averaging, edges stay hard: this is the correct tool where a blur-and-threshold would round corners and shift boundaries. Extended to greyscale by replacing containment with min and max, the same operators give local minimum and maximum filters, and the difference between dilation and erosion — the morphological gradient — is an edge detector with no smoothing. In generation this is the machinery of mask cleanup: removing single-cell speckle from a cellular-automata cave, closing one-tile gaps in a corridor, growing a wall by exactly two tiles, and separating touching blobs by repeated erosion.
algorithms.citation: Serra, Image Analysis and Mathematical Morphology, Academic Press, 1982; founded with Matheron at the École des Mines de Paris from 1964

algorithms.name: Midpoint displacement / diamond-square
algorithms.authors: Alain Fournier, Don Fussell, Loren Carpenter
algorithms.summary: Recursively subdivide and randomly offset midpoints to approximate fractional Brownian motion. Detail to any depth without storing it.
algorithms.eli5: Draw a straight line between two points. Find its middle and shove it up or down by a random amount. Now you have two shorter lines — do the same to each, but shove them only half as far. Repeat, and a mountain profile grows out of one straight line.
algorithms.description: Seed the four corners of a grid. The diamond step sets each square's centre to the average of its four corners plus a random offset; the square step sets each diamond's centre to the average of its four neighbours plus a random offset. Halve the offset range each round and recurse. How fast that range decays is the roughness parameter, and it corresponds to the Hurst exponent of the resulting surface — which is what ties the algorithm to real terrain, since measured landscapes have fractal roughness. The visible flaw is that the grid axes leak through as faint creases, because corner values are reused along rows and columns far more than diagonally.
algorithms.citation: Computer rendering of stochastic models, Communications of the ACM 25(6), 371–384

algorithms.name: Karplus–Strong string synthesis
algorithms.summary: A delay line of noise fed back through a one-pole averager. A plucked string from about four lines of code.
algorithms.eli5: Fill a short loop of memory with random noise and play it round and round. Each time round, average every sample with the one beside it. The noise loses its harshness a little at a time, with the highest pitches dying first — which is exactly what a plucked string does.
algorithms.description: Fill a buffer of N samples with noise. Then repeatedly: output the oldest sample, and push back onto the buffer the average of that sample and the next one. The buffer length sets the pitch — the fundamental is the sample rate divided by N. The averaging is a low-pass filter applied once per period, so high harmonics lose energy far faster than low ones, which is exactly what a real string does as it decays. The initial noise burst supplies all harmonics at once, standing in for the pluck. It is startling how much instrument comes out of a delay line and an average, and it is the canonical demonstration that physical modelling beats sampling for variation.
algorithms.citation: Digital synthesis of plucked-string and drum timbres, Computer Music Journal 7(2), 43–55

algorithms.name: Liang hyphenation patterns
algorithms.summary: A packed trie of letter patterns with odd/even scores. Hyphenates correctly in a few kilobytes, no dictionary.
algorithms.eli5: How does a computer know that "hyphenation" splits as hy-phen-a-tion? Not by knowing any words. Someone fed a dictionary through a program that extracted thousands of tiny letter patterns, each with a score for and against breaking there. Add up the scores at each gap, and the odd totals win.
algorithms.description: Rather than store a dictionary, Liang extracted patterns: short letter sequences, each carrying digits that vote for or against a break at each position. Odd values encourage a hyphen, even values forbid one, and higher values override lower. To hyphenate a word, match every pattern that occurs in it, take the maximum vote at each inter-letter position, and break where the result is odd. The pattern set is generated automatically from a hyphenated dictionary by a greedy procedure that repeatedly adds whichever patterns fix the most remaining errors, and it is stored in a packed trie of a few kilobytes. Note this is not a Markov model despite being learned from a corpus — the catalogue tags it `markov`, which is wrong; it is deterministic pattern matching with no probabilities at all.
algorithms.citation: Liang, Word Hy-phen-a-tion by Com-put-er, Stanford PhD thesis, 1983

algorithms.name: Mip pyramid / pyramidal parametrics
algorithms.summary: Precompute a chain of half-size copies of a field so any scale can be read in constant time.
algorithms.eli5: Keep the picture, then a copy at half the width, then a copy at half of that, all the way down to a single dot. When something is far away you read from a small copy instead of averaging thousands of pixels from the big one. It costs a third more memory and turns an expensive question into one lookup.
algorithms.description: Build successive levels by averaging each 2×2 block, halving resolution each time, until a single sample remains. Because each level is a correctly band-limited version of the one above, sampling at the level matching the screen footprint gives a filtered result without touching more than a few samples, and blending between two levels — trilinear filtering — hides the transition. The total cost is 4/3 of the original, since 1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + … converges. For generation this is more than a rendering trick: the pyramid is a multi-scale decomposition of a field, so a mip chain over a heightfield gives cheap access to "average slope at kilometre scale", which is what biome rules, LOD selection and erosion pre-passes actually want. Williams introduced it as a solution to texture aliasing; its use as a general field summary came later.
algorithms.citation: Williams, Pyramidal parametrics, Computer Graphics (SIGGRAPH 83) 17(3), 1–11

algorithms.name: Simulated annealing
algorithms.authors: Scott Kirkpatrick, C. Daniel Gelatt, Mario Vecchi
algorithms.summary: Accept worsening moves with a probability that falls over time. Escapes local optima early, converges late.
algorithms.eli5: Hill-climbing gets stuck on the first little hill it finds. So allow yourself to step *downhill* sometimes — often at the start, rarely later, on a cooling schedule. Early on you roam and find the big hills; later you settle and climb. It is named after cooling metal slowly so its crystals form properly.
algorithms.description: Borrowed directly from metallurgy: cool a metal slowly and its atoms settle into a low-energy crystal; quench it and they freeze into defects. The optimisation analogue proposes a random change to the current solution, always accepts it if it improves the objective, and accepts it anyway with probability exp(−Δ/T) if it worsens. The temperature T starts high, so early on the search wanders almost freely and cannot get trapped, then falls on a cooling schedule until only improvements are accepted. The cooling schedule is the whole art — too fast and it quenches into a poor local optimum, too slow and it costs more than exhaustive search. It needs no gradient, no population and barely any memory, which is why it is the default when you have a scoring function and an awkward discrete space, such as level layout or timetable repair.
algorithms.citation: Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi, Optimization by Simulated Annealing, Science 220(4598), 671–680

algorithms.name: D8 flow direction and accumulation
algorithms.summary: Send each cell's water to its steepest of eight neighbours, then count how many cells drain through each. Rivers appear as a threshold.
algorithms.eli5: Each square on the map sends all its water to whichever of its eight neighbours is steepest downhill. Follow the arrows and you can count, for every square, how many squares upstream eventually drain through it. Squares with a big count are rivers; the biggest counts are the mouth.
algorithms.description: Assign each cell one of eight directions — the neighbour with the steepest downward drop, with diagonal distances scaled by √2. That single choice per cell turns the heightfield into a forest of trees rooted at the outlets, and accumulating cell counts up those trees gives contributing area: the number of cells whose water passes through each cell. Thresholding accumulation is the standard way to extract a channel network, and the threshold is effectively the drainage density dial. The method's limitation is built into the name: with only eight directions, flow on a planar hillside cannot spread and instead collapses into parallel lines one cell wide, which is what D-infinity and multiple-flow-direction schemes exist to fix. It is nonetheless the foundation everything else in the concept sits on, it requires depressions to have been filled first, and it is what lets a generated terrain place rivers, lakes, valleys and settlements from the heightfield alone.
algorithms.citation: O'Callaghan & Mark, The extraction of drainage networks from digital elevation data, Computer Vision, Graphics and Image Processing 28(3), 323–344

algorithms.name: Summed-area table
algorithms.summary: Store running sums so the total of any axis-aligned rectangle costs four lookups regardless of its size.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of storing each square's number, store the total of everything above and to the left of it. Now the sum of any rectangle is four of those totals added and subtracted — the big one, minus the two overhangs, plus the corner you subtracted twice. A blur over a thousand-pixel box costs exactly the same as one over a three-pixel box.
algorithms.description: Each entry holds the sum of every sample above and to the left of it, computed in one pass. The sum over any axis-aligned rectangle is then S(x2,y2) − S(x1,y2) − S(x2,y1) + S(x1,y1): four reads, constant time, independent of the rectangle's size. That turns a box blur into an O(1)-per-pixel operation and, since a box blur applied three times approximates a Gaussian, makes large-radius blurs affordable. The catch is numerical: the running sums grow with area, so a large field in 32-bit floats loses precision at the far corner, which is why implementations use integers or tiles. Beyond blurring, it is the standard way to answer "how much of this is there, in this region" — local averages for adaptive thresholding, coverage for scattering rules, and the feature evaluation inside classic object detectors.
algorithms.citation: Crow, Summed-area tables for texture mapping, Computer Graphics (SIGGRAPH 84) 18(3), 207–212

algorithms.name: Perlin noise
algorithms.summary: Gradient noise on an integer lattice. Built in 1983 out of frustration with how machine-like Tron looked; Academy Award 1997.
algorithms.eli5: At every corner of a grid, pin a tiny arrow pointing a random way. To get the value somewhere in between, ask each nearby corner's arrow "am I in the direction you are pointing?" and blend the answers. Because neighbouring corners agree along the edge they share, the result is smooth everywhere and you never see the grid.
algorithms.description: Every point of an integer lattice gets a pseudo-random unit gradient vector, derived by hashing its coordinates so no storage is needed and the result is the same everywhere, forever. To evaluate a sample, take the vector from each surrounding lattice corner to the sample point, dot it with that corner's gradient, and interpolate the results using a smooth ease curve. Because every gradient is dotted with a zero-length offset at its own corner, the function is exactly zero at every lattice point — which is the source of the faint axis-aligned grid that Perlin noise never entirely loses. Perlin's 2002 'Improving Noise' fixed two details: a fifth-order interpolant with zero second derivative at the ends, and a restricted gradient set that removes directional bias.
algorithms.citation: An Image Synthesizer, SIGGRAPH '85

algorithms.name: Value noise
algorithms.authors: No single origin; contemporaneous with Perlin noise
algorithms.summary: Hash a random value at each lattice point and interpolate between them. Cheaper and blobbier than gradient noise.
algorithms.eli5: Write a random number at every corner of a grid and fade smoothly between them. Simpler than the arrow version — but the random numbers sit exactly on the corners, so the grid shows through as a faint pattern of blobs.
algorithms.description: Assign a pseudo-random scalar to every lattice point by hashing its coordinates, then interpolate between the surrounding values with a smooth ease curve. That is the whole algorithm — it is what most people write first when asked to make smooth noise.
