The difference from Perlin noise is that Perlin stores gradients and takes dot products, so its value is zero at every lattice point and the extrema fall between them; value noise stores the values directly, so extrema land exactly on the lattice. The consequence is a more visible grid and a blobbier, lower-frequency character. It is cheaper, and for many uses — scattering weights, low-frequency variation, jitter — the difference is invisible and not worth the cost. No paper introduced it; it is the obvious construction, and it circulated as practice.
algorithms.citation: No origin publication. Documented in Ebert et al., Texturing & Modeling: A Procedural Approach.

algorithms.name: FLIP
algorithms.summary: Hybrid particle-grid fluid: particles carry the state, a grid solves the pressure. Splashy without dissipating.
algorithms.eli5: Two ways of tracking fluid, glued together. Particles remember where the water is and which way it was going, because particles never blur. A grid does the shoving needed to stop the water squashing, because that sum needs neighbours in fixed places. Every step, hand the information from one to the other and back again.
algorithms.description: Pure grid methods lose detail because interpolating velocity each frame smears it — the fluid looks viscous when it should not. Pure particle methods struggle to enforce incompressibility. FLIP takes both: transfer particle velocities to a background grid, solve the pressure projection there to make the field divergence-free, then transfer the *change* in velocity back to the particles rather than the velocity itself. Because only the delta is interpolated, the particles retain their own high-frequency motion and nothing is smoothed away. That single choice is why FLIP looks energetic and splashy where its predecessor PIC looks like syrup, and blending between the two is the standard viscosity dial in production fluid solvers.
algorithms.citation: Brackbill & Ruppel, FLIP: A method for adaptively zoned, particle-in-cell calculations of fluid flows in two dimensions, J. Computational Physics 65(2), 314–343

algorithms.name: Fortune's sweepline
algorithms.summary: Sweeps a line across the plane maintaining a parabolic beach line, emitting Voronoi vertices as arcs vanish. O(n log n).
algorithms.eli5: Rather than work out every patch at once, drag a line across the page from left to right and only settle each patch as the line reaches it. What trails behind the line is a wobbly curve, and the corners of the finished diagram appear exactly where that curve crosses itself.
algorithms.description: Sweep a horizontal line down the plane. Behind it, maintain the 'beach line': a sequence of parabolic arcs, each the locus of points equidistant from one already-passed site and from the sweep line. Anything behind the beach line has its Voronoi cell finalised, because no future site can be closer. Two event types drive it — a site event, where the sweep line reaches a new point and inserts an arc, and a circle event, where an arc is squeezed to nothing between its neighbours and a Voronoi vertex is emitted at the circumcentre. Both structures are balanced trees, giving O(n log n) time and O(n) space, which is optimal. The cleverness is the beach line: it converts a global nearest-neighbour problem into a local one.
algorithms.citation: A sweepline algorithm for Voronoi diagrams, Proc. 2nd Annual Symposium on Computational Geometry, 313–322 (also Algorithmica 2, 1987)

algorithms.name: Boids
algorithms.summary: Three steering rules per agent — separation, alignment, cohesion — and flocking emerges with no leader.
algorithms.eli5: Give every bird three rules: do not bump into your neighbours, point roughly the way they are pointing, and drift towards the middle of the ones near you. Nobody leads and nobody plans. A flock happens anyway.
algorithms.description: Each agent looks only at neighbours within a local radius and applies three steering urges: separation, to avoid crowding; alignment, to match their average heading; cohesion, to move toward their average position. Sum them, weight them, clamp to a maximum force, and integrate. Nothing computes the flock — there is no leader, no global plan, and no agent knows the flock exists — yet the aggregate motion is convincingly organic, splits around obstacles and rejoins. Reynolds' framing mattered as much as the rules: he presented it as an alternative to scripting each bird's path, which is the general argument for emergent generation over authored content. The tuning trap is that the three weights interact non-linearly; too much cohesion collapses the flock to a point, too much separation disperses it entirely, and the pleasing band between them is narrow.
algorithms.citation: Reynolds, Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model, SIGGRAPH '87, Computer Graphics 21(4), 25–34

algorithms.name: BSP-tree set operations
algorithms.summary: Union, difference and intersection evaluated by merging BSP trees. Exact boolean modelling on arbitrary polyhedra.
algorithms.eli5: To cut one solid out of another, you must know which parts of each surface lie inside the other. So chop both solids into pieces, using each other's walls as knives, until every piece is unambiguously inside or outside. Then throw away the pieces you do not want and glue what remains back together.
algorithms.description: Represent each solid as a BSP tree whose leaves are labelled inside or outside — this is an exact representation of an arbitrary polyhedron, not an approximation. A boolean is then computed by merging one tree into the other: push the second solid's tree down through the first's planes, splitting it as it goes, and combine the in/out labels at the leaves according to the operation. Because everything is decided by which side of a plane a region lies on, the result is topologically exact and closed by construction. This is the classical answer to why CSG is easier than mesh booleans: mesh-based approaches have to compute intersection curves between surfaces and stitch them, which is numerically fragile, whereas BSP reduces the whole problem to plane classification.
algorithms.citation: Thibault & Naylor, Set operations on polyhedra using binary space partitioning trees, SIGGRAPH '87, Computer Graphics 21(4), 153–162

algorithms.name: Katz back-off
algorithms.summary: When an n-gram was never seen, fall back to the shorter context rather than assigning zero probability.
algorithms.eli5: The three-letter run you need never appeared in your list, so its chance looks like zero and everything grinds to a halt. The fix: shave a little probability off every run you *did* see, and hand the pooled leftovers down to the shorter two-letter guess. Ask for three, fall back to two, fall back to one.
algorithms.description: Raw n-gram counts assign probability zero to anything unobserved, which is fatal — a single unseen bigram makes an entire generated sequence impossible. Katz back-off discounts the observed counts slightly, freeing a mass of probability, then redistributes it by falling back to the (n−1)-gram model whenever the full context has too few observations to trust. The fallback recurses down to unigrams. The practical effect for a name generator or a text model is that it can produce combinations absent from the corpus while still preferring ones the corpus supports — which is exactly the balance between plagiarism and gibberish that determines whether generated names feel authentic.
algorithms.citation: Estimation of probabilities from sparse data for the language model component of a speech recogniser, IEEE Trans. ASSP 35(3), 400–401

algorithms.name: Marching cubes
algorithms.summary: Turns a sampled scalar field into a triangle mesh by table lookup, one cube at a time. The most cited paper in computer graphics.
algorithms.eli5: You have a big block of numbers and you want the surface where they cross zero. Look at each little cube of eight numbers and ask which corners are inside and which are outside. There are only 256 possible answers, so look up the right little patch of triangles in a table, and stitch all the patches together.
algorithms.description: Sample the field on a regular grid. For each cube of eight neighbouring samples, each corner is either inside or outside the isosurface, giving 256 possible sign configurations — reduced to 15 distinct cases by rotation and reflection symmetry, and baked into a lookup table of triangle topologies. For each edge that crosses the surface, linearly interpolate along it to find where the field hits the threshold, and emit the triangles the table specifies. It is fast, embarrassingly parallel, and needs no global information, which is why it is everywhere. Two known weaknesses: sharp creases get rounded off, because vertices only ever land on cube edges; and several configurations are genuinely ambiguous, producing holes unless a disambiguation scheme is added.
algorithms.citation: Marching cubes: A high resolution 3D surface construction algorithm, SIGGRAPH '87, Computer Graphics 21(4), 163–169

algorithms.name: Marching squares
algorithms.authors: No origin publication; the 2D specialisation of marching cubes
algorithms.summary: Trace the contour line where a field crosses a threshold, one grid cell at a time, from a 16-case table.
algorithms.eli5: You have a grid of numbers and want to draw the line where they cross, say, ten. Look at each little square of four numbers and ask which corners are above ten and which are below. There are only sixteen possible answers, so look up which way the line cuts through, and stitch all the little line segments together.
algorithms.description: For each cell of four samples, the four above-or-below bits index a table of 16 configurations giving the line segments crossing that cell. Linear interpolation along the cut edges places each endpoint at the actual crossing rather than at the cell boundary, which is the difference between a smooth isoline and a staircase. Two of the sixteen cases are saddles where the four corners alternate, and the table has to pick a joining — a genuine ambiguity, usually resolved by testing the cell centre. This is the machinery behind contour maps, shaded relief, coastline extraction from a heightfield, and the outline of any 2D metaball or SDF blob. It has no origin paper because it is the two-dimensional restriction of marching cubes, and was in use before anyone thought it needed naming separately.
algorithms.citation: No origin paper. The 2D case of Lorensen & Cline's marching cubes (1987); the ambiguous saddle cases and their resolution are discussed throughout the isosurface literature.

algorithms.name: Answer set programming
algorithms.summary: Declare rules and constraints in logic; the solver returns stable models — every valid world, not just one.
algorithms.eli5: Describe the world as rules of the form "this holds if those hold, unless that is known". Then ask not for a yes-or-no answer but for every complete self-consistent world in which all your rules are true. Each of those worlds is one valid generated artefact.
algorithms.description: Write a logic program of rules and integrity constraints. Its stable models — the answer sets — are exactly the consistent worlds satisfying it, and a solver enumerates them. The distinctive feature for content generation is that it produces *all* valid solutions rather than one, which makes it possible to sample uniformly from the space of legal artefacts instead of taking whatever a search happens to reach first. It also supports default reasoning: rules can hold unless contradicted, which maps naturally onto design constraints of the form 'rooms connect to corridors unless they are secret'. Answer set programming has a real if small following in PCG research — Smith and Mateas argued for it as a general framing where the designer writes what must be true and the solver handles the rest.
algorithms.citation: Gelfond & Lifschitz, The stable model semantics for logic programming, ICLP/SLP 1988, 1070–1080

algorithms.name: Iterated function systems
algorithms.summary: A handful of contractive affine maps applied at random. Their attractor is a fractal — the Barnsley fern from four transforms.
algorithms.eli5: Write down three or four rules that each shrink and tilt a picture. Start with a single dot, pick a rule at random, apply it, and repeat a million times, leaving a mark each time. The marks pile up into a fern — and that fern is the only picture those rules could ever have drawn.
algorithms.description: Take a small set of affine transformations, each of which contracts distances. Whatever shape you start from, applying the set repeatedly converges to a single attractor determined entirely by the transforms — Hutchinson's theorem — so the fractal is fully specified by a few rows of numbers. The chaos game evaluates it cheaply: start at any point, repeatedly pick one transform at random with assigned probabilities, apply it, and plot the result. After discarding the first few iterations the points land on the attractor and nowhere else. Barnsley's fern needs four transforms, one of which is applied only one per cent of the time to make the stem. The compression implication was the original excitement: an image reduced to twenty-four numbers.
algorithms.citation: Barnsley, Fractals Everywhere, Academic Press, 1988; Hutchinson, Fractals and self similarity, Indiana Univ. Math. J. 30, 1981

algorithms.name: Musgrave hydraulic and thermal erosion
algorithms.authors: F. Kenton Musgrave, Craig Kolb, Robert Mace
algorithms.summary: The first erosion pass applied to fractal terrain. Water carries sediment downhill; talus slides until it is below the angle of repose.
algorithms.eli5: Two passes over a landscape. The first drops rain on every cell and lets it pick up soil, run downhill, and put the soil down again wherever it slows. The second simply checks whether any slope is steeper than loose dirt can stand and, if so, tips material down until it is not. Rivers from the first, scree from the second.
algorithms.description: Two separate processes run over a heightfield. Thermal erosion handles material loosened and falling: for each cell, compare height with its neighbours, and wherever the slope exceeds a fixed talus angle, move a fraction of the difference downhill. Repeated, this produces the constant-angle scree slopes real cliffs accumulate at their base. Hydraulic erosion adds water: each cell holds some water and dissolved sediment, water flows to lower neighbours carrying sediment with it, sediment beyond the water's capacity is deposited, and some water evaporates each step. The result is drainage — connected channels, deposition in valleys — which is exactly the structure that pure fractal noise cannot have, and why this paper marks the point terrain stopped looking like crumpled paper.
algorithms.citation: The synthesis and rendering of eroded fractal terrains, SIGGRAPH '89, Computer Graphics 23(3), 41–50

algorithms.name: Cyclic coordinate descent (CCD)
algorithms.summary: Rotate one joint at a time to aim the end effector at the target, walking back from the tip. One equation, one unknown.
algorithms.eli5: Work backwards from the hand. Rotate the wrist so that the hand points as close to the target as it can manage. Then do the same at the elbow, then the shoulder. Then go round again. It always converges, needs no mathematics harder than an angle — and tends to over-bend whichever joint is nearest the target.
algorithms.description: Start at the joint nearest the end effector. Rotate that joint by the single angle that best aligns the vector from joint to end effector with the vector from joint to target — a one-line calculation from the angle between two vectors. Move to the next joint down the chain and repeat, then loop back to the tip and go again. Each step reduces the error monotonically, and each involves one degree of freedom, so there is nothing to invert and nothing to tune. It converges quickly for short chains and is trivial to implement, which is why it is everywhere in games. Its characteristic artefact is that joints near the end effector absorb most of the rotation, giving a curled, over-bent wrist unless you weight or limit the per-joint rotation.
algorithms.citation: A combined optimization method for solving the inverse kinematics problem of mechanical manipulators, IEEE Trans. Robotics and Automation 7(4), 489–499

algorithms.name: Eigenfaces (PCA shape models)
algorithms.summary: Principal component analysis over aligned faces. The eigenvectors become the sliders.
algorithms.eli5: Average a thousand photographed faces, then ask what the main ways real faces differ from that average are. Out come a few dozen ghostly difference-pictures. Any face is now the average plus a pinch of the first, a dash of the second, and so on — a face has become a list of a few dozen numbers.
algorithms.description: Treat each aligned face image as a point in a very high-dimensional space — one dimension per pixel — and run principal component analysis over a population of them. The leading eigenvectors are directions of greatest variation, and they turn out to be interpretable: overall lightness, then broad shape, then progressively finer structure. Any face is then approximated by the mean plus a weighted sum of a few dozen components, so a whole face is described by a few dozen numbers. This is the ancestor of every morphable model that followed, and it establishes the pattern the whole `morph` concept rests on: don't write rules for what a face can be, measure a population and let the principal components be the parameters. Its limits are equally instructive — everything must be aligned first, and pushing the weights beyond the range seen in the data produces monsters.
algorithms.citation: Turk & Pentland, Eigenfaces for Recognition, J. Cognitive Neuroscience 3(1), 71–86

algorithms.name: Marching tetrahedra
algorithms.summary: Split each cube into tetrahedra before contouring, removing marching cubes' ambiguous cases.
algorithms.eli5: The cube version has a few awkward cases where you genuinely cannot tell how the surface should join up. The fix: chop each cube into tetrahedra first. A tetrahedron has four corners, so there are barely any cases and none of them is ambiguous. You get more and uglier triangles in exchange for never having to guess.
algorithms.description: Marching cubes has configurations where the sign pattern at the eight corners does not determine the surface topology, and choosing wrongly leaves holes between adjacent cells. Marching tetrahedra sidesteps this by decomposing each cube into five or six tetrahedra first. A tetrahedron has only four corners and therefore just two distinct cases up to symmetry — one corner separated, or two-and-two — and neither is ambiguous, so the resulting mesh is always watertight. The cost is roughly three times as many triangles for the same field, and a visible bias in triangle orientation from the fixed decomposition. It is the usual choice when correctness matters more than triangle count, and the reason it appears in GPU and differentiable pipelines is that the case table is small enough to branch on cheaply.
algorithms.citation: Doi & Koide, An efficient method of triangulating equi-valued surfaces by using tetrahedral cells, IEICE Trans. Information and Systems E74-D(1), 214–224

algorithms.name: Mitchell's best-candidate
algorithms.summary: Generate k random candidates, keep the one furthest from existing samples. Approximate blue noise in five lines.
algorithms.eli5: To place a dot nicely, do not just pick a spot. Pick ten random spots and keep whichever one is furthest from every dot already placed; bin the other nine. Almost embarrassingly simple, and the result looks scattered by hand.
algorithms.description: To add a point, generate k random candidates and keep whichever is furthest from any already-placed sample. Increasing k improves the blue-noise quality and the cost; k around ten is the usual compromise. It is strictly worse than Bridson's method on both spectral quality and asymptotic cost, but it fits in a few lines, needs no background grid, works over any domain you can sample and measure distance in — including surfaces and non-uniform densities — and never fails to place a point. That last property matters: Poisson disk sampling with a fixed radius can simply run out of room, whereas best-candidate degrades gracefully. It is the right choice when you want approximately even scatter without infrastructure.
algorithms.citation: Mitchell, Spectrally optimal sampling for distribution ray tracing, SIGGRAPH '91, Computer Graphics 25(4), 157–164

algorithms.name: Genetic programming
algorithms.summary: Evolve programs rather than parameter strings. Individuals are expression trees, and crossover swaps subtrees.
algorithms.eli5: The same breed-and-select loop, except what you are breeding is little programs shaped like trees, not lists of numbers. Splicing two survivors means swapping a branch of one tree for a branch of the other, so the offspring is a working program that nobody wrote and nobody has read.
algorithms.description: Instead of a fixed-length chromosome, each individual is a program — usually an expression tree over a chosen function and terminal set. Crossover swaps randomly chosen subtrees between two parents, and mutation replaces a subtree with a fresh random one. Because the representation is variable-size, the search explores structures rather than just parameter values, which is what lets it discover the *form* of a solution and not merely tune one. In generation this is how you evolve shaders, textures, plant grammars, and behaviour trees — the classic result being that evolved expressions produce imagery nobody would have written by hand. Its characteristic pathology is bloat: trees grow ever larger with introns that do nothing, because neutral code is protective against destructive crossover, so implementations need explicit size pressure.
algorithms.citation: Koza, Genetic Programming: On the Programming of Computers by Means of Natural Selection, MIT Press, 1992

algorithms.name: Material point method
algorithms.authors: Deborah Sulsky, Zhen Chen, Howard Schreyer; brought into graphics by Stomakhin, Schroeder, Chai, Teran & Selle
algorithms.summary: Particles carry material state, a grid computes forces. Handles snow, sand, mud and goo in one solver.
algorithms.eli5: Little points carry what the material *is* — how squashed, how cracked, how wet. A background grid does the pushing, because pushing needs to know what is next to what. The points hand their state to the grid, the grid works out the forces, and the points collect the answer and move. One solver covers snow, sand, mud and jelly.
algorithms.description: A continuum method on a hybrid representation: particles hold mass, velocity and — crucially — a deformation gradient recording how the material around them has been stretched and sheared since rest. Each step transfers state to a background grid, computes forces there from a constitutive model applied to the deformation gradient, updates velocities, and transfers back. Changing the constitutive model changes the material without changing the solver, which is why one implementation covers snow, sand, mud, foam and viscoelastic goo. Stomakhin's paper added elastoplasticity with hardening — snow compacts as it deforms and stops springing back — and was written for Disney's *Frozen*, which is a good illustration of production driving the research rather than the reverse. Its lineage matters and is easy to miss: MPM was built as an extension of FLIP — already in this table — from fluids to solid mechanics, the addition being that each particle carries the full stress tensor so that history-dependent constitutive models become possible. The 2013 snow paper is what made it famous in graphics, and is where the sand, mud and goo variants come from, but the method is nineteen years older than that.
algorithms.citation: Sulsky, Chen & Schreyer, A particle method for history-dependent materials, Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 118, 179–196 (1994). Graphics introduction: Stomakhin et al., A material point method for snow simulation, ACM TOG 32(4) (SIGGRAPH 2013)

algorithms.name: Ridged multifractal
algorithms.summary: Invert the absolute value of each noise octave and weight it by the previous one. Sharp ridges, not rounded hills.
algorithms.eli5: Take a layer of noise and fold it: wherever it dips below zero, flip it back up. Smooth valleys become sharp creases. Stack several folded layers, and let each one only show up where the layer above was already high, and you get ridgelines with side spurs instead of rounded hills.
algorithms.description: Take the absolute value of a signed noise octave and subtract it from one. The absolute value creates a crease wherever the noise crosses zero, and inverting turns that crease into a ridge rather than a valley. Summed across octaves this gives sharp crests — mountain ridgelines, mineral veins, lightning-like filaments — where plain fBm gives rounded lumps. Musgrave's addition beyond the basic trick is the multifractal part: weight each octave by the value of the previous one, so detail only appears where the coarser scale was already high. That is what makes the ridges sharp on peaks and the valleys smooth, which is how real terrain behaves and what plain fBm gets wrong by applying the same roughness everywhere. Published in the Texturing & Modeling book rather than as a paper.
algorithms.citation: Musgrave, in Ebert, Musgrave, Peachey, Perlin & Worley, Texturing & Modeling: A Procedural Approach, Academic Press, first edition 1994 — a book chapter, not a paper.

algorithms.name: Delaunay refinement
algorithms.authors: Jim Ruppert, building on L. Paul Chew (1989)
algorithms.summary: Insert circumcentres of bad triangles until every angle clears a bound. Meshes with a mathematical quality guarantee.
algorithms.eli5: You have triangles, but some are horrible skinny splinters that make simulations go wrong. Find the worst one, drop a brand-new point right at the centre of its circle, and re-triangulate. No splinter survives that. Keep going until nothing is too thin — and it can be proved that this always stops.
algorithms.description: A Delaunay triangulation of scattered points contains slivers — thin triangles that wreck numerical simulation. Refinement fixes this by adding points: find any triangle whose smallest angle falls below a threshold, insert its circumcentre as a new vertex, and re-triangulate. Each insertion destroys the offending triangle, and the surprising result is that the process terminates rather than cascading forever, with the mesh size within a constant factor of optimal. Chew's 1989 technical report established the first such guarantee at 30°; Ruppert extended it to graded meshes with varying element size and boundary constraints. This is why FEM and CFD meshes can be generated automatically at all, and it is the same insertion idea used to grade Voronoi cell sizes for procedural districts.
algorithms.citation: Ruppert, A Delaunay refinement algorithm for quality 2-dimensional mesh generation, J. Algorithms 18(3), 548–585; Chew, Guaranteed-quality triangular meshes, Cornell TR 89-983

algorithms.name: Kneser–Ney smoothing
algorithms.summary: Back off on how many distinct contexts a word appears in, not how often it appears. The best-performing n-gram smoothing.
algorithms.eli5: "Francisco" is a common word, but almost only ever after "San". So when guessing what follows an unfamiliar phrase, do not ask how *often* a word appears — ask in how many *different* company it has been seen. Words that only ever turn up inside one phrase get demoted, which is why this beats every other counting method.
algorithms.description: Ordinary back-off falls back to raw unigram frequency, which misfires on words that are common but contextually narrow. The stock example is 'Francisco': it appears often, but almost only after 'San', so backing off to its frequency makes it a plausible continuation everywhere, which it is not. Kneser–Ney instead builds the lower-order distribution from *continuation counts* — how many distinct contexts a word has followed — so 'Francisco' scores low despite being frequent. Combined with absolute discounting, subtracting a fixed amount from every observed count, it reliably gives the lowest perplexity of any n-gram method. For generation it is the difference between a name generator that produces convincingly varied output and one that keeps emitting the same few high-frequency fragments.
algorithms.citation: Kneser & Ney, Improved backing-off for m-gram language modeling, ICASSP 1995, 181–184

algorithms.name: Social force model
algorithms.summary: Pedestrians as particles under fictitious social forces — a drive toward the goal, repulsion from others and walls.
algorithms.eli5: Treat a walking person as though invisible springs and magnets were acting on them — pulled towards where they want to go, pushed away from other people and from walls. Add up the pushes and pulls and take a step. Crowds jam in doorways and form lanes in corridors without anyone being told to.
algorithms.description: Treat each pedestrian as a point mass under three kinds of force. An acceleration term drives them toward their desired velocity — the direction and speed they want to be going. Repulsive terms push them away from other pedestrians and from walls, falling off exponentially with distance and weighted by whether the obstacle is in front of them. Attractive terms pull toward things they want to approach. Integrate and crowds emerge: lanes form spontaneously in bidirectional flow, arch-shaped jams appear at doorways, and at high density the model reproduces the faster-is-slower effect where increasing individual urgency reduces total throughput. That last result is why the model is used seriously for evacuation planning and venue design rather than just for making crowds look busy.
algorithms.citation: Helbing & Molnár, Social force model for pedestrian dynamics, Physical Review E 51(5), 4282–4286

algorithms.name: Straight skeleton
algorithms.authors: Oswin Aichholzer, Franz Aurenhammer, David Alberts, Bernd Gärtner
algorithms.summary: Shrink a polygon by moving every edge inward at constant speed; the traces of the vertices form the skeleton. Solves roofs from a footprint.
algorithms.eli5: Shrink a shape by sliding every wall inwards at the same speed at once. Watch the corners: as they move they trace out lines. Those lines are the skeleton — and they are exactly where the ridges and valleys of a roof would fall if you put a roof on that outline.
algorithms.description: Move every edge of the polygon inward, parallel to itself, at the same constant speed. Each vertex travels along its angle bisector, and the paths those vertices trace out are the straight skeleton. Two things interrupt the shrinking: an edge event, where an edge collapses to zero length and its neighbours become adjacent, and a split event, where a reflex vertex crashes into an opposite edge and cuts the polygon in two. Unlike the medial axis it contains only straight segments, never arcs. Its use in architecture falls straight out of the definition: if you lift the shrinking wavefront vertically at a constant rate, the surface swept is a roof of uniform pitch, so hip and gable roofs come free from the building footprint.
algorithms.citation: A novel type of skeleton for polygons, J. Universal Computer Science 1(12), 752–761

algorithms.name: Open L-systems
algorithms.summary: L-systems extended with bidirectional information exchange with the environment, so growth responds to light, space and competition.
algorithms.eli5: The plant above is blind: its branches grow through walls and through each other. Here the turtle may stop and ask questions. Is there light at this spot? Is there already a branch here? The answers come back from a separate program that models the world, and the plant grows around whatever it finds.
algorithms.description: Ordinary L-systems are closed — the rules cannot see anything outside the string, which is why naive trees grow branches through each other and through the trunk. Open L-systems add query modules: special symbols that the turtle interpretation writes environmental data into, such as the light reaching that position or whether the space is already occupied. An external environment program reads the plant's current geometry, computes the answers, and writes them back; the next derivation step then has rules that branch on those values. Growth becomes a conversation rather than a monologue, which is what makes shade avoidance, pruning and competition between neighbouring plants expressible at all.
algorithms.citation: Visual Models of Plants Interacting with Their Environment, SIGGRAPH '96

algorithms.name: Wilson's algorithm
algorithms.summary: Generates a uniformly random spanning tree by loop-erased random walks. Every possible maze equally likely.
algorithms.eli5: Every other maze method is biased — it produces some shapes more often than others. This one is not. Pick a cell not yet in the maze, wander at random erasing your own loops whenever you cross your path, and when you finally bump into the maze, carve the walk you were left holding.
algorithms.description: Pick any vertex and call it the tree. Then repeatedly: choose a vertex not yet in the tree and random-walk from it, erasing loops as they form — if the walk revisits its own path, cut out the loop and carry on from that point. When the walk finally touches the tree, add the whole loop-erased path to it. Repeat until every vertex is in. The result is drawn uniformly from all spanning trees of the graph, which matters because the popular alternatives are biased: recursive backtracker produces long snaking corridors with few junctions, Prim's produces bushy short-branched ones, and neither samples the space of mazes evenly. Wilson's is slower to start — early walks wander a long time before finding the small tree — but it is the only simple algorithm that is genuinely unbiased.
algorithms.citation: Generating random spanning trees more quickly than the cover time, Proc. 28th ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, 296–303

algorithms.name: Worley / cellular noise
algorithms.summary: Distance to the nth nearest feature point. F1 and F2 give cells, cracks, scales and caustics. Written explicitly as a complement to Perlin noise.
algorithms.eli5: Scatter dots. For any spot, answer with the distance to the nearest dot. You get a floor of cells with a ridge wherever two dots are equally close — which is what cracked mud, stone and the skin of an orange look like.
algorithms.description: Scatter feature points through space — in practice one or a few per grid cell, jittered, so only the 27 neighbouring cells need checking. For a sample point, compute the sorted distances to nearby features: F1 is the nearest, F2 the second nearest. F1 alone gives rounded cell blobs that darken toward each seed. F2 minus F1 is near zero exactly on the boundary between two cells, so it draws the cracks — which is where flagstones, scales, dried mud and crackle come from. Changing the distance metric changes the cell shape: Euclidean gives organic cells, Manhattan and Chebyshev give angular, crystalline ones.
algorithms.citation: A Cellular Texture Basis Function, SIGGRAPH '96, 291–294

algorithms.name: D-infinity flow routing
algorithms.summary: Give each cell a continuous downslope angle and split its water between the two neighbours either side of it.
algorithms.eli5: Sending all the water to one of eight neighbours forces every stream onto a compass direction, so hillsides end up striped with parallel lines. Instead, work out the true downhill direction — any angle at all — and split the water between the two neighbours it points between, in proportion to how close it is to each. Flow can now spread out and fan the way it really does.
algorithms.description: Fit eight triangular facets to each cell and its neighbours, take the steepest downslope direction across all of them as a continuous angle, then apportion flow between the two cardinal or diagonal neighbours bracketing that angle in proportion to the angular distance. The result keeps the single-direction methods' ability to converge into channels while allowing divergence on hillslopes and fans, which is what D8 structurally cannot do — its artefact is parallel single-cell flow lines on any planar slope. Accumulation becomes a weighted sum over a directed acyclic graph rather than a tree, so it still computes in one topological pass. For terrain generation the difference shows exactly where it matters most: alluvial fans, deltas, braided channels and the broad wetted areas that make a valley floor read as a floodplain rather than as a single scratched line.
algorithms.citation: Tarboton, A new method for the determination of flow directions and upslope areas in grid digital elevation models, Water Resources Research 33(2), 309–319

algorithms.name: Quadric error metric decimation
algorithms.summary: Collapse the edge whose removal moves the surface least, measured by a per-vertex quadratic form. The standard LOD algorithm.
algorithms.eli5: To simplify a shape, merge two nearby corners into one. But which pair, and where should the merged corner go? Give every corner a little formula that says how much error you would cause by putting it anywhere. Add the two formulas together, solve for the spot with the least error, and always merge whichever pair is cheapest. Repeat until the shape is as simple as you asked for.
algorithms.description: Each vertex carries a 4×4 symmetric matrix — the sum of outer products of the plane equations of its incident faces — which evaluates, for any candidate position, the total squared distance to those original planes. Collapsing an edge adds the two matrices, and minimising the resulting quadratic is a small linear solve giving both the optimal merged position and the error incurred. Put every candidate collapse in a priority queue by that error, pop the cheapest, collapse, and update the affected neighbours. Because the error is accumulated rather than recomputed against the original mesh, cost stays low while quality stays high, and the same formulation extends to preserving colour and UVs by widening the quadric. This is what almost every automatic LOD chain, mesh budget tool and game-engine importer runs, which makes it the algorithm that decides what generated geometry looks like at distance — and its known failure mode is that it will happily collapse a thin feature that lies close to its own plane.
algorithms.citation: Garland & Heckbert, Surface simplification using quadric error metrics, SIGGRAPH 97, 209–216

algorithms.name: Exact geometric predicates
algorithms.summary: Adaptive-precision arithmetic that makes orientation and in-circle tests exact, so boolean and meshing code stops crashing.
algorithms.eli5: Every geometry algorithm rests on questions like "is this point to the left of that line?". With ordinary computer arithmetic the answer is occasionally wrong by a hair, and one wrong answer makes the whole algorithm produce nonsense. The cure is arithmetic that is exact when it has to be — and that can cheaply tell when it has to be.
algorithms.description: Mesh booleans, Delaunay triangulation and BSP construction all rest on two questions: which side of a plane is this point on, and is this point inside that circumsphere. Both are determinant signs, and in floating point a near-degenerate input can return the wrong sign — producing not a slightly wrong answer but an inconsistent topology, which is why boolean modelling has a reputation for fragility. Shewchuk's method computes these predicates exactly using expansions of floating-point values, and does so adaptively: compute a fast approximate result first with an error bound, and only escalate to more precision when the bound cannot decide the sign. In the overwhelming majority of cases the cheap path suffices, so exactness costs almost nothing on average. This is the substrate under CGAL, Triangle and most robust CSG in production.
algorithms.citation: Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates, Discrete & Computational Geometry 18(3), 305–363

algorithms.name: Bilateral filter
algorithms.summary: Blur, but only average samples that are similar in value as well as close in space. Smooths without crossing edges.
algorithms.eli5: An ordinary blur smears across every boundary, so a sharp line goes soft. Fix it with one extra rule: only average a neighbour in if its value is also close to yours. Then flat areas get smoothed and edges are left alone, because the pixels on the far side of an edge never get a vote.
algorithms.description: Multiply the usual spatial weight by a second weight based on how different the neighbour's value is from the centre's, and normalise. Two parameters — a spatial radius and a value tolerance — control how far it looks and how much difference it will tolerate. The result is that gradients are smoothed while steps survive, which is why it underlies denoising, tone mapping, cartoon shading and the "detail layer" split used throughout texture authoring: bilateral-filter a heightfield, subtract, and you have separated the large forms from the fine grain without the halos a Gaussian split produces. It is not separable and naively costs O(r²) per pixel, which drove a decade of accelerations — the bilateral grid, the permutohedral lattice, and the guided filter, which achieves the same edge-aware behaviour in linear time. Its known artefact is gradient reversal near strong edges, visible as a thin halo when the detail layer is amplified.
algorithms.citation: Tomasi & Manduchi, Bilateral filtering for gray and color images, ICCV 1998, 839–846

algorithms.name: Mersenne Twister
algorithms.summary: Period 2^19937−1 and 623-dimensional equidistribution from 624 words of state. The default PRNG almost everywhere.
algorithms.eli5: A dice machine that keeps 624 numbers as its memory and stirs them with shifts and exclusive-ors. It will not repeat itself for an unimaginably long time and its numbers pass the statistical tests people cared about in 1998. Big, slow to start, and never to be used where somebody might want to cheat.
algorithms.description: A twisted generalised feedback shift register. State is 624 32-bit words; each step combines two words far apart in the array with a bit-mixing 'twist' matrix, then passes the result through a tempering transform of shifts and masks to flatten the output distribution. The period is a Mersenne prime, 2^19937−1, and it is provably equidistributed in up to 623 dimensions at 32-bit precision — meaning consecutive outputs cover high-dimensional space uniformly, which is the property Monte Carlo integration actually needs. Its weaknesses are practical rather than statistical: 2.5 KB of state is large, recovering from a poor seed takes a long time, and observing 624 outputs reveals the entire internal state, so it is unsuitable anywhere unpredictability matters.
algorithms.citation: Mersenne Twister: A 623-dimensionally equidistributed uniform pseudo-random number generator, ACM Trans. Modeling and Computer Simulation 8(1), 3–30

algorithms.name: Surface nets
algorithms.summary: One vertex per surface-crossing cell, relaxed to smooth the mesh while constrained to stay inside its own cell. The first dual contouring method.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of cutting triangles inside every cube, put one single point in each cube the surface passes through, then tug each point towards where the surface really crosses. Join the points of neighbouring cubes into quads. Far fewer and much better-shaped polygons — at the cost of softening every corner.
algorithms.description: Where marching cubes places vertices on cube edges, surface nets places exactly one vertex inside each cube that the surface passes through, and connects vertices in neighbouring cubes to form quads — the dual arrangement. The vertex positions are then relaxed iteratively, each one pulled toward the average of its linked neighbours to smooth the mesh, but clamped so it can never leave its original cube. That constraint is what stops the smoothing from shrinking the model away. It produces far better-shaped triangles than marching cubes and no ambiguous cases, at the cost of rounding sharp features even harder.
algorithms.citation: Constrained Elastic Surface Nets: Generating Smooth Surfaces from Binary Segmented Data, MICCAI '98

algorithms.name: 3D Morphable Model
algorithms.summary: PCA over registered 3D face scans, separating shape from texture. The basis of every parametric face system since.
algorithms.eli5: The same idea in three dimensions, with scanned heads instead of photographs. Line every scan up so the tip of each nose is the same point, average them, and find the main ways they vary. Now a slider means something real — rounder, longer, older — and every setting is still a head a person could have.
algorithms.description: Take a set of 3D face scans and put them in dense correspondence, so that vertex n means the same anatomical point on every face — that registration step is most of the work, and it is what makes the linear algebra meaningful. Then run PCA separately over shape and over texture, giving two independent parameter spaces. New faces are linear combinations of the principal components, and because shape and texture are separated you can vary skin independently of bone structure. The paper also showed the inverse direction: fit the model's parameters by analysis-by-synthesis until the rendered face matches a photograph, recovering a 3D face from a single image. That fitting idea is the ancestor of modern photo-to-avatar pipelines, and the model's descendants — Basel, FLAME, SMPL for bodies — are the same construction with better data.
algorithms.citation: Blanz & Vetter, A morphable model for the synthesis of 3D faces, SIGGRAPH '99, 187–194

algorithms.name: Stable fluids
algorithms.summary: An unconditionally stable Navier–Stokes solver that never blows up regardless of timestep. Made real-time smoke practical.
algorithms.eli5: Smoke simulations used to explode the moment you took a big time step. The fix: instead of asking where each puff of smoke goes next, ask where each grid cell's smoke must have come *from*, and go and fetch it. Fetching can never overshoot, so it can never explode — you only lose a little swirl.
algorithms.description: Explicit fluid solvers explode if the timestep is too large relative to the grid — the CFL condition — which made interactive fluid impossible. Stam's method splits each step into stages that are each unconditionally stable: advection is done by semi-Lagrangian backtracing, tracing backwards from each grid cell to find where its contents came from and interpolating there, which can never produce a value outside the existing range and therefore cannot diverge; diffusion and pressure projection are solved implicitly as linear systems. The price is numerical dissipation — semi-Lagrangian advection smooths the field every step, so vorticity fades and smoke looks too smooth, which is why vorticity confinement was invented to add the lost swirl back. It is the paper that put fluid into games.
algorithms.citation: Stam, Stable Fluids, SIGGRAPH '99, 121–128

algorithms.name: Shuffle bags and pity timers
algorithms.authors: Game development practice; no single origin
algorithms.summary: Reshape a random distribution so it feels fair. Draw without replacement, or raise the odds after each failure.
algorithms.eli5: Real randomness feels unfair — it will happily hand you the same item five times running. So put one of each item in a bag, draw without putting them back, and refill only when it is empty. Now you get all of them, in a random order. A pity timer is the same idea for rare drops: quietly raise the odds every time you miss.
algorithms.description: Uniform random produces streaks, and players experience streaks as broken rather than random. Two standard corrections. A shuffle bag holds one token per possible outcome, draws without replacement, and refills when empty — so over each cycle every outcome appears exactly its intended number of times and long droughts are impossible; Tetris piece generation is the canonical case. A pity timer instead raises the probability of a rare outcome on each consecutive failure, so the drop rate is low early and approaches certainty at the cap, giving a bounded worst case; this is what most gacha and loot systems actually run, and the headline percentage they advertise is the average over that ramp rather than a per-roll constant. Neither is documented in a paper, and both matter more to perceived quality than almost any generator in the catalogue.
algorithms.citation: Game development practice. No canonical publication; described in GDC talks and design writing.

algorithms.name: Squarified treemaps
algorithms.authors: Mark Bruls, Kees Huizing, Jarke van Wijk
algorithms.summary: Subdivides a rectangle into weighted sub-rectangles that stay close to square, instead of thin slivers.
algorithms.eli5: You have a rectangle and a list of numbers, and each number must get an area that size. Laying them out in strips gives horrible long slivers, so instead keep adding items to the current strip only while doing so keeps the shapes closer to square — then start a fresh strip.
algorithms.description: The original slice-and-dice treemap alternates horizontal and vertical cuts, which preserves ordering but produces long thin slivers that are hard to compare or click. The squarified variant instead greedily adds items to a row while the worst aspect ratio in that row keeps improving, and starts a new row as soon as it would get worse — laying rows along the shorter side of the remaining space. The result approximates squares, at the cost of no longer preserving input order. In generation it is the standard trick for subdividing a footprint into rooms or a block into building lots with sensible proportions, because a room of area A that is 1×A is useless and a room that is √A×√A is a room.
algorithms.citation: Bruls, Huizing & van Wijk, Squarified Treemaps, Proc. Joint Eurographics / IEEE TCVG Symposium on Visualization, 33–42

algorithms.name: Cassowary
algorithms.authors: Greg Badros, Alan Borning, Peter Stuckey
algorithms.summary: Incremental linear constraint solver with hard and soft constraints. The engine under Auto Layout.
algorithms.eli5: Layout as a tug of war. State what must be true — this panel sits eight pixels right of that one — and what you would merely prefer, each preference with a strength. When the window resizes, the solver re-satisfies every must and abandons the weakest preferences first, without redoing the whole calculation.
algorithms.description: An incremental variant of the dual simplex method built for interactive use: constraints are added and removed one at a time and the solution is repaired rather than recomputed, so it keeps up with a window being dragged. Its second contribution is a constraint hierarchy — constraints carry strengths, from required down through strong, medium and weak, and the solver satisfies all required ones while minimising violation of the rest by preference order. That is what makes it usable for layout, where 'this panel must be inside the window' is non-negotiable but 'these two should be equal width' is a preference that yields when space runs short. It is the solver behind Apple's Auto Layout and a great many web and GUI layout engines, which makes it one of the most widely executed constraint solvers in existence.
algorithms.citation: Badros, Borning & Stuckey, The Cassowary linear arithmetic constraint solving algorithm, ACM TOCHI 8(4), 267–306

algorithms.name: CMA-ES
algorithms.summary: Evolution strategy that learns the shape of the search landscape by adapting a full covariance matrix.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of a population, keep a cloud: a centre point, plus a description of which directions the cloud is stretched in. Sample from it, see which samples did well, shift the centre towards them and re-stretch the cloud along whichever directions have been paying off. It learns the shape of the landscape while descending it.
algorithms.description: Sample a population from a multivariate Gaussian, evaluate, and then update not just the mean but the *covariance matrix* of that Gaussian from the successful samples — so the distribution stretches along directions that have been paying off and shrinks across directions that have not. It also maintains an evolution path, a smoothed record of where the mean has been moving, which lets it distinguish a genuine trend from noise and adapt the overall step size accordingly. The effect is that it learns the local scaling and correlation structure of the problem, making it near-invariant to how the parameters happen to be scaled or rotated — the practical reason it works on badly conditioned problems where plain evolution strategies stall. It is the default choice for continuous, derivative-free optimisation up to a few hundred dimensions.
algorithms.citation: Hansen & Ostermeier, Completely Derandomized Self-Adaptation in Evolution Strategies, Evolutionary Computation 9(2), 159–195

algorithms.name: L-system road networks
algorithms.summary: L-systems grow street networks from population and terrain maps, then shape grammars build the lots and buildings. Became CityEngine.
algorithms.eli5: The turtle draws roads instead of branches. At each step it consults two maps — how many people live around here, and what shape is the ground — then decides whether to carry straight on, swing round to follow a ridge, or split in two. Big roads get drawn first; small streets fill in the blocks they leave behind.
algorithms.description: An L-system proposes road segments, but every proposal passes through two filters before it is accepted. Global goals shape the overall pattern — follow population density gradients, or impose a grid, radial or organic street style. Local constraints then adjust the individual segment: snap its endpoint to a nearby intersection if it is close enough, shorten it to stop at water, reject it if the slope is impossible. That propose-then-correct loop is what stops the network looking like a fractal and makes it look surveyed. Once the road graph closes, the enclosed blocks are recursively subdivided into lots with street frontage, and a shape grammar builds a mass on each lot.
algorithms.citation: Procedural Modeling of Cities, SIGGRAPH '01

algorithms.name: Simplex noise
algorithms.summary: Replaces the hypercube lattice with a simplex grid, cutting corner count from 2^n to n+1. Fewer artefacts, far better scaling into 3D and 4D.
algorithms.eli5: The same trick as Perlin noise, played on a grid of triangles instead of squares. A triangle has fewer corners to ask, so it is faster, and it loses the square grid's habit of showing faint streaks along the axes.
algorithms.description: The cost of classic Perlin noise doubles with every dimension, because a hypercube in n dimensions has 2^n corners that all need interpolating. Simplex noise skews the input coordinates onto a lattice of simplices — the simplest shape that tiles a space, a triangle in 2D and a tetrahedron in 3D — which has only n+1 corners. Contributions from each corner are summed with a radial falloff rather than interpolated along axes, so there is no axis-aligned interpolation to leave grid artefacts. Complexity drops from O(2^n) to O(n²), which is what makes 4D noise (3D plus time, for animated volumes) practical at all. Perlin patented it, which is why OpenSimplex exists as an unencumbered alternative.
algorithms.citation: Noise Hardware, in Real-Time Shading SIGGRAPH Course Notes, 2001

algorithms.name: Tessendorf ocean spectra
algorithms.summary: Synthesise ocean surface in the frequency domain from an empirical wave spectrum, then inverse FFT to a heightfield.
algorithms.eli5: The sea is not a set of waves you can draw. It is a recipe: for each wave size and direction, how much of it there is, measured from real oceans. Add thousands of those waves together in one enormous shortcut and out comes a patch of sea surface that looks right because it was measured, not invented.
algorithms.description: Rather than simulating water, synthesise a height field whose statistics match measured ocean. Start in the frequency domain: fill a complex grid with Gaussian random values scaled by the Phillips spectrum, an empirical model of how wave energy distributes across wavelength and direction given wind speed and fetch. Animate by rotating each frequency's phase according to the dispersion relation, which is what makes long waves travel faster than short ones — the detail that separates convincing ocean from moving noise. An inverse FFT returns the heightfield. Adding a horizontal displacement derived from the same spectrum produces Gerstner-like sharpened crests. It is the standard for both film and games, and it is a clear case of imitating measured statistics rather than deriving from physics.
algorithms.citation: Tessendorf, Simulating Ocean Water, SIGGRAPH course notes (1999–2004) — course notes, not a peer-reviewed paper

algorithms.name: Dual contouring
algorithms.authors: Tao Ju, Frank Losasso, Scott Schaefer, Joe Warren
algorithms.summary: Positions one vertex per cell by least-squares fitting the surface normals on its edges, so sharp edges and corners survive.
algorithms.eli5: Like the above, one point per cube — except you choose where that point goes by asking which way all the little surface fragments crossing this cube are facing, and solving for the spot that suits them all. If a genuine sharp edge runs through the cube, the solution lands exactly on it, so hard edges survive.
algorithms.description: Like surface nets it puts one vertex per cell, but it decides where by using Hermite data — not just where the surface crosses each edge, but the surface normal at that crossing. Each crossing defines a plane the surface should lie on; the vertex is placed at the point minimising squared distance to all of them, solved as a small least-squares system. Where the crossings agree the solution is a flat patch; where two or three planes meet at an angle the minimiser lands exactly on the crease or corner. That is the whole trick: normals carry the information that positions alone lose, so a cube comes out of the field as a cube rather than a rounded lump. The quadratic form can be degenerate on flat regions and needs regularising.
algorithms.citation: Dual contouring of Hermite data, ACM Transactions on Graphics 21(3) (SIGGRAPH 2002)

algorithms.name: Least-squares conformal maps
algorithms.authors: Bruno Lévy, Sylvain Petitjean, Nicolas Ray, Jérome Maillot
algorithms.summary: Flatten a surface into UV space by solving one sparse linear system that minimises angular distortion.
algorithms.eli5: You want to peel a 3D surface flat so you can paint on it, like flattening an orange skin. You cannot do it without stretching, so decide what to protect: keep every corner's *angles* as close to right as possible, and let the sizes stretch. That turns out to be one big set of simultaneous equations, and solving it once gives the whole flattening.
algorithms.description: Conformal maps preserve angles locally. Writing the discrete Cauchy–Riemann condition per triangle and minimising its squared violation over the whole chart gives a sparse least-squares problem, linear in the unknown UV coordinates, solvable in one shot once two vertices are pinned to remove the translation, rotation and scale freedom. There is no iteration and no per-triangle nonlinear solve, which is why it was the method that made automatic UV unwrapping practical. Angles are preserved but areas are not, so long thin charts can scale wildly along their length, and the pinned vertices influence the result — both addressed by later methods (ABF++, ARAP, and area-aware variants). For generated geometry this is the step that makes a procedural mesh texturable at all, and it is why the practical pipeline is: cut the surface into charts, flatten each with something like LSCM, then pack the charts into an atlas.
algorithms.citation: Lévy, Petitjean, Ray & Maillot, Least squares conformal maps for automatic texture atlas generation, ACM TOG 21(3) (SIGGRAPH 2002), 362–371

algorithms.name: Weighted Voronoi stippling
algorithms.summary: Lloyd relaxation weighted by image darkness, so stipple density follows tone.
algorithms.eli5: You want to redraw a photograph as thousands of ink dots, crowded in the shadows. Scatter dots, give each the region of the picture nearest to it, then move each dot to the *darkness-weighted* middle of its region. Repeat, and the dots migrate into the dark areas by themselves.
algorithms.description: Scatter points over the image, then run Lloyd relaxation — but instead of moving each point to the geometric centroid of its Voronoi cell, move it to the centroid weighted by image darkness, treating pixel intensity as a density function. Points therefore drift toward dark regions and spread apart in light ones. After a few iterations the stipple density reproduces the source tone while the spacing stays even and non-gridded, which is precisely what a human stippler achieves by eye. It is a neat demonstration that a single change of weighting turns a geometric relaxation into a tone-reproduction algorithm.
algorithms.citation: Weighted Voronoi Stippling, NPAR 2002, 37–43

algorithms.name: Fractal flames
algorithms.summary: IFS with non-linear variations, log-density tone mapping and structural colouring. The Apophysis look.
algorithms.eli5: The same dot-and-random-rule game, but bendy rules are allowed as well as shrinking ones, and instead of merely marking each spot you count how many times it was visited. Bright where the dots crowd, dim where they wander, which is why these look lit rather than drawn.
algorithms.description: Three changes to a plain iterated function system, each responsible for part of the aesthetic. First, the affine maps are composed with non-linear 'variations' — sinusoidal, spherical, swirl and dozens more — so the attractor curves and folds instead of staying piecewise-linear. Second, rather than plotting points as binary hits, accumulate a density histogram and tone-map it logarithmically, which preserves detail across the enormous dynamic range between the dense core and the faint outer wisps. Third, carry a colour coordinate along with each point, updated by whichever transform was applied, so hue encodes the history of the trajectory rather than its position. Together they turn a mathematical curiosity into the most recognisable style in generative art.
algorithms.citation: The Fractal Flame Algorithm, 2003 (revised 2008)

algorithms.name: Poisson image editing
algorithms.authors: Patrick Pérez, Michel Gangnet, Andrew Blake
algorithms.summary: Paste a region by matching its gradients, not its values, and solving for the values that fit. Seams disappear.
algorithms.eli5: Pasting a patch into a picture leaves a visible edge because the patch's brightness does not match its surroundings. So do not paste the brightnesses at all — paste only the *changes* from pixel to pixel, and then work backwards to find the brightnesses that both produce those changes and match the border exactly. The patch shifts its own tone to fit, and the seam vanishes.
algorithms.description: Take the gradient field of the source region as the target, fix the values on the boundary to those of the destination, and solve for the interior values whose gradient best matches — which is a Poisson equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions, one sparse linear solve per channel. Because only gradients are transferred, absolute intensity is free to shift, so the inserted region relights itself to its new surroundings and the seam disappears without any feathering. Variants fall out of manipulating the guidance field rather than the solver: mixing source and destination gradients pastes transparent or textured content, zeroing selected gradients removes objects, and amplifying them enhances local contrast. In procedural work this is the general answer to joining generated tiles or patches whose overall levels differ — the gradient-domain half of seam removal, complementary to the pixel-selection half that graph-cut textures solve.
algorithms.citation: Pérez, Gangnet & Blake, Poisson image editing, ACM TOG 22(3) (SIGGRAPH 2003), 313–318

algorithms.name: Potrace
algorithms.summary: Bitmap to vector: trace boundaries, fit an optimal polygon, then smooth into Bézier curves.
algorithms.eli5: Turning a pixel drawing into smooth curves, in three passes. First trace the staircase outline of the black pixels. Then work out the longest straight-ish runs that staircase could have stood for, and join them into a polygon. Finally round the polygon's corners into curves. Each pass throws away one kind of pixelness.
algorithms.description: Three stages. First decompose the bitmap into closed paths along the boundaries between black and white, using a consistent turn policy so ambiguous diagonal crossings resolve the same way everywhere. Second, approximate each path by an optimal polygon — optimal in the sense of minimising the number of segments subject to each segment staying within the pixel boundary, solved as a shortest-path problem rather than greedily, which is what stops the output looking stair-stepped. Third, classify each polygon vertex as a corner or a smooth point and fit Bézier segments accordingly, so curves come out curved and corners stay sharp. It is the standard raster-to-vector path, and the middle stage — global optimisation rather than local fitting — is the part that distinguishes it from naive tracers.
algorithms.citation: Selinger, Potrace: a polygon-based tracing algorithm, 2003

algorithms.name: Xorshift
algorithms.summary: Three shifts and three XORs. Among the fastest usable generators, and small enough to inline.
algorithms.eli5: The entire generator is three lines: shift the number, exclusive-or it with itself, three times over with different shift amounts. That is all of it. Wildly fast, small enough to memorise, and only just good enough — it fails some of the harder statistical tests, which is why its descendants add a final scramble.
algorithms.description: The state is a single machine word. Each step XORs the state with a shifted copy of itself, three times, with a carefully chosen triple of shift amounts — the choice determines whether the generator achieves its full period of 2^k−1. That is the entire algorithm: no multiplication, no memory beyond one register, and it compiles to a handful of instructions. Plain xorshift fails some statistical tests because the output is a linear function of the state over GF(2), which later scrambled variants (xorshift*, xoshiro) fix by applying a non-linear output transform. For procedural generation the appeal is that it is cheap enough to run per-pixel or per-voxel without thinking about cost.
algorithms.citation: Xorshift RNGs, Journal of Statistical Software 8(14), 1–6

algorithms.name: Droplet erosion
algorithms.authors: No single origin; many independent variants
algorithms.summary: Drop individual particles on the heightfield and let each carve its own path downhill.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of flooding the whole map at once, drop one raindrop somewhere and follow it. It rolls downhill, scooping up dirt as it speeds up and dropping it as it slows, until it dries up. Do that a million times with a million drops and valleys and rivers carve themselves.
algorithms.description: Instead of solving flow over the whole grid, spawn a droplet at a random point and follow it. It accelerates down the local gradient, picks up sediment in proportion to its speed and the steepness, deposits when it slows or when carrying more than its capacity, loses a little water to evaporation each step, and dies after a fixed lifetime. Run a few hundred thousand droplets and drainage networks emerge. It is far simpler to implement than grid-based hydraulic erosion and needs no global solve, which is why it dominates hobbyist and indie terrain code; the trade-off is that results depend on droplet count and seeding, and it is harder to reason about convergence. There is no origin paper — it is a simplification of the Musgrave and Mei models that spread through tutorials and blog posts.
algorithms.citation: No canonical publication. A particle simplification of grid hydraulic erosion; widely reimplemented from tutorials.

algorithms.name: Euclidean rhythms (Bjorklund)
algorithms.authors: Godfried Toussaint; algorithm by Eric Bjorklund
algorithms.summary: Distribute k onsets as evenly as possible over n beats using the Euclidean algorithm. Reproduces a great many traditional rhythms.
algorithms.eli5: Spread five beats as evenly as you can across sixteen slots. It does not divide, so use the ancient trick for finding a greatest common divisor and it spreads the awkwardness out evenly instead of dumping it at the end. Out come the rhythms of a startling number of traditional drum patterns.
algorithms.description: Given n beats and k onsets, the problem is to space the onsets as evenly as possible when k does not divide n. Bjorklund's algorithm — originally written for timing pulses in a neutron spallation source — solves it by the same repeated-remainder structure as Euclid's GCD: pair off groups of the two sequence types, recursing on the remainder, until at most one group is left over. Toussaint's contribution was the observation that the resulting patterns coincide with a striking number of traditional rhythms across West African, Latin American, Balkan and Middle Eastern music. E(3,8) is the tresillo, E(5,8) the cinquillo, E(5,16) the Brazilian bossa-nova pattern. Worth noting the catalogue overclaims this as producing 'most world rhythms'; Toussaint's claim is that many traditional rhythms are Euclidean, not most.
algorithms.citation: Toussaint, The Euclidean Algorithm Generates Traditional Musical Rhythms, Proc. BRIDGES 2005, 47–56

algorithms.name: Falling-sand automata
algorithms.authors: No single origin; formalised in Noita's Falling Everything engine
algorithms.summary: Per-pixel material simulation by local swap rules. Sand falls, water spreads, fire consumes fuel.
algorithms.eli5: Every grain of sand looks at the square below it. Empty? Fall. Blocked? Try down-left, then down-right. That is sand. Now say water also spreads sideways, fire turns neighbouring wood into fire, and water on fire makes steam — and you have a whole physics out of a handful of if-statements.
algorithms.description: Every pixel holds a material, and each is updated by rules that only inspect its immediate neighbours: sand moves down, or diagonally down if blocked; water does the same but also spreads sideways; gas rises; fire converts flammable neighbours and burns out. Ordering matters more than the rules do — updating a grid top-to-bottom makes falling material teleport in a single frame, so implementations scan bottom-up for falling materials, alternate scan direction per frame to remove left-right bias, and mark cells dirty to skip settled regions. It is not a cellular automaton in the strict sense, because updates are sequential and in-place rather than simultaneous, which is exactly what allows conservation of material. Noita's engine is the most complete realisation and the reason the technique is taken seriously as a game mechanic rather than a toy.
algorithms.citation: No origin paper. Nolla Games' Falling Everything engine is the reference implementation; described in their GDC talk.

algorithms.name: Reiter snowflake model
algorithms.summary: A two-parameter cellular automaton on a hexagonal grid producing genuinely six-fold dendritic snow crystals.
algorithms.eli5: Fill a honeycomb of hexagons with water vapour and freeze the middle one. Then repeat one rule: a hexagon freezes when enough of its neighbours already have, and freezing sucks the vapour out of the area around it. Arms grow, starve their own flanks, and split — which is why real snowflakes have six arms and no two match.
algorithms.description: Cells sit on a hexagonal lattice and hold a real value representing water. Cells adjacent to the frozen crystal are 'receptive'; their water is held and not diffused, and a constant addition term feeds them. All non-receptive cells diffuse toward the average of their neighbours. Each step, receptive cells that exceed one become part of the crystal. Just two parameters — the background vapour level and the addition constant — select the entire morphology, sweeping through plates, dendrites, stellar and sectored forms in a way that matches the real Nakaya diagram surprisingly well. It is a good example of a model that is genuinely mechanistic rather than imitative: the six-fold symmetry emerges from the lattice and the diffusion, and is not imposed.
algorithms.citation: A local cellular model for snow crystal growth, Chaos, Solitons & Fractals 23, 1111–1119

algorithms.name: Wavelet noise
algorithms.summary: Near-perfectly band-limited noise, fixing the aliasing and detail loss Perlin noise suffers under minification.
algorithms.eli5: Ordinary noise grows extra sparkle when you shrink it and goes mushy when you enlarge it. This version is built by blurring a random picture, subtracting the blur from the original and keeping only the difference, so every size of detail lives in its own drawer and cannot leak into another.
algorithms.description: Perlin noise is not actually band-limited — each octave leaks energy into frequencies above and below its nominal band. Minify it and the high leakage aliases into visible crawling; blur it and the low leakage means detail vanishes before it should. Wavelet noise fixes this by construction: generate a tile of random values, downsample it by half, upsample that back to full size, and subtract the result from the original. What remains is precisely the content that could not survive a halving — a single, clean octave band. Summing such bands with correct scaling gives noise where each octave can be faded in and out independently as the surface changes size on screen, which is what makes it hold up under both minification and projection of 3D noise onto a 2D surface.
algorithms.citation: Wavelet noise, ACM Transactions on Graphics 24(3), 803–811 (SIGGRAPH 2005)

algorithms.name: CGA shape grammars
algorithms.authors: Pascal Müller, Peter Wonka, Simon Haegler, Andreas Ulmer, Luc Van Gool
algorithms.summary: A split grammar for buildings: mass to floors to facade tiles to windows, with context-sensitive rules.
algorithms.eli5: A building starts as a plain box. One rule slices it into floors, the next slices each floor into bays, the next says a bay is a wall with a hole in it, and the last drops in a window. Because every rule works on whatever the previous rule made, a whole city comes out of a page of rules.
algorithms.description: Rules operate on labelled scopes — an oriented box with a coordinate frame. A rule either subdivides a scope along an axis into labelled child scopes, repeats a component across it, or replaces it with geometry. So a building mass splits into floors, a floor's front face splits into a row of facade tiles, a tile splits into window, sill and wall, and a window is finally instantiated as an asset. Context sensitivity is what lifted it above earlier split grammars: rules can query occlusion and neighbouring scopes, so a facade knows not to place a window where another building abuts it, and ground floors can differ from upper ones. Müller's team rebuilt Pompeii with it, and it became CityEngine. This is the archetype for the whole `architecture` domain of the catalogue.
algorithms.citation: Müller et al., Procedural modeling of buildings, ACM TOG 25(3) (SIGGRAPH '06), 614–623

algorithms.name: Jump flooding
algorithms.summary: Propagate nearest-seed information across a grid in log n passes with halving step sizes. Voronoi and distance fields on the GPU.
algorithms.eli5: Every square needs to know which seed is nearest. Ask the squares that are 64 steps away, then 32, then 16, then 8, and so on down to 1 — each time keeping the best seed you have heard about. After a handful of rounds everyone knows, and every square did its asking at the same moment as every other.
algorithms.description: Seed cells with their own coordinates and leave the rest empty. Then for step sizes n/2, n/4, … 1, each cell looks at its eight neighbours at that offset and keeps whichever candidate seed is closest to itself. Information travels a long way in the first passes and is refined in the last, so the whole field converges in log n rounds rather than the n rounds flood-filling would take. Every cell is independent within a pass, which is the point: this is how you compute a Voronoi diagram or a distance field on a GPU, where a sequential sweep would be worthless. It is approximate — a small number of cells can end up with the wrong nearest seed — and the paper quantifies the error, which is low enough that jump flooding is the standard technique for real-time SDF generation, soft shadows from silhouettes, and outline effects.
algorithms.citation: Rong & Tan, Jump flooding in GPU with applications to Voronoi diagram and distance transform, I3D 2006, 109–116

algorithms.name: Poisson surface reconstruction
algorithms.authors: Michael Kazhdan, Matthew Bolitho, Hugues Hoppe
algorithms.summary: Treat oriented points as samples of a surface gradient and solve for the field whose gradient best matches them.
algorithms.eli5: You have a cloud of measured points, each with a little arrow saying which way is 'out'. Rather than joining the points up, look for the smooth in-or-out field across all of space whose own arrows best agree with the measured ones. Solve that once, then take the surface where the field crosses the middle. Noise and holes get smoothed over for free, because you asked for the best global fit rather than a local join.
algorithms.description: The indicator function of a solid — one inside, zero outside — has a gradient that is zero everywhere except at the surface, where it is the inward normal. Reverse that: given oriented sample points, build a vector field approximating that gradient, then find the scalar field whose gradient best matches it in the least-squares sense. Taking the divergence turns this into a Poisson equation, discretised on an adaptive octree with a hierarchy of smooth basis functions and solved with a multigrid method, after which the surface comes out by isosurfacing. Because the formulation is global, noise averages out and holes are filled by the smoothest plausible continuation rather than by a local heuristic — the property that made it the default in photogrammetry and LiDAR pipelines and put it inside MeshLab, CloudCompare and Open3D. The trade is that it never reproduces a sharp crease exactly, and it will confidently close a hole that should have stayed open.
algorithms.citation: Kazhdan, Bolitho & Hoppe, Poisson surface reconstruction, Eurographics Symposium on Geometry Processing 2006, 61–70

algorithms.name: Bridson Poisson disk sampling
algorithms.summary: Blue-noise point sets in O(N) and in any dimension, by throwing darts only near existing samples.
